💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that as a lifelong cyclist, I’ve received well-intentioned bicycle-themed presents that sit around unused, get forgotten in my closet, or are regifted or donated years later.
  • According to recent reports, admittedly, buying gifts for cyclists isn’t always easy, and every bicycle rider is different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Sources indicate that as a lifelong cyclist, I’ve received well-intentioned bicycle-themed presents that sit around unused, get forgotten in my closet, or are regifted or donated years later. If you’re shopping for a Christmas or birthday gift for a bike rider, buy something they will truly appreciate and actually use.

According to recent reports, admittedly, buying gifts for cyclists isn’t always easy, and every bicycle rider is different. Cycling is often an expensive, gear-heavy activity with many niches and sub-categories, each with particular equipment needs. Resist the temptation to buy a T-shirt with a poorly drawn bike, AI-generated artwork, or a novelty cycling jersey. Instead, choose something they will love. You can find great gifts that show you put in the extra effort, won’t break your budget, or take weeks to arrive.

In a recent development, here’s a list of 20 of the most helpful, beautiful, fun, and affordable gifts for cyclists under $50; items we’ve tested, loved, and rely on. Want even more great deals on cycling gear and accessories? Bookmark our Best Bike Gear Deals page for sales and discounts from top cycling retailers.

Sources indicate that bells are handy on the bike path, around town, and on the trail. Aussie brand Knog’s Oi bell is discreet, looks good on everything from a commuter to a race bike, and weighs only about 25 grams. Pick up the Oi Classic with a glass-fiber lever or step up to the Oi Luxe with a metal hammer for about $20 more.

Lezyne makes some of our favorite cycling lights for commuting, road, gravel, and mountain biking. However, while super bright and durable, the brand’s lights can be a bit costly. The KTV Drive combo is a lightweight set of front and rear lights to keep riders visible on commutes and in urban environments. They’re rechargeable, have up to 40 hours of runtime, and fit most bikes.

Recent findings suggest that electric mini inflators have taken the cycling world by storm. These devices let you quickly and precisely air up any bike tire. However, most inflators are a bit too large and heavy to carry in a jersey pocket or seat bag. Although the Pocket SE doesn’t have a pressure gauge, this pint-sized inflator weighs only 90 grams and fills up to four tires per charge.

According to recent reports, the Duraglove ETs from Defeet are an awesome addition to any rider’s fall and winter cycling wardrobe. They’re perfect for rides where temperatures are still above freezing but not warm enough to go without gloves. These gloves have rubber grippers (for holding your handlebar in wet conditions) and are touchscreen-compatible with your smartphone or head unit. They’re an excellent value for under $25.

Sometimes the best gifts are high-end versions of normal things you wouldn’t buy for yourself. While only 33 grams and the size of an Allen key, Daysaver’s Essential8 has the same wrenches as your regular multitool. The design uses nested and flippable magnetic bits made from high-quality stainless steel. As a bonus gift, the Essential8 pairs perfectly with the Coworking5 extension.

Sources indicate that what started as a homemade, low-sugar, all-natural sports drink is now a player in cycling nutrition. Skratch Labs offers a palatable solution that keeps you hydrated and energized without causing tummy aches. The brand’s formula is designed to replace exactly what you lose through heavy sweating, whether riding outdoors or on the indoor trainer. Skratch offers several flavors (like lemon-lime, orange, pineapple, and more) and seasonal ones (like apple cider).

Sources indicate that want to save weight in your tires or space in your seat bag? TPU tubes are lighter than traditional butyl rubber tubes and roll faster. They also pack down to about half the size of traditional inner tubes, so they’re the perfect spare tube for your flat kit. They’re available in sizes that fit most road, gravel, and mountain bikes.

It has been revealed that we were skeptical that $40 shorts could be this good. However, the Black Bibs consistently outperform shorts that cost six times as much. They’re very simple—no fancy fabrics or creative cuts—and that’s why we love them. Made entirely of plain black Lycra with mesh straps and large leg grippers at the cuffs, they don’t look like anything special. However, even after logging over a year in the Black Bibs, one tester consistently reaches for them first.

Sources indicate that toe covers are perfect for days when it’s not quite cold enough for full booties, but you want to keep your toes warm on the ride. Pearl Izumi’s Amfib model is a solid pick; plus, they are reflective for rides after dark. They provide enough stretch to fit over most road shoes (with cleats) and are easy to put on and take off.

Industry observers note that the small but mighty Mattone is a great choice for sleek, waterproof, and secure storage. Thanks to its elastic material, you can pack it to the gills or keep a minimal setup and cinch it tight with the Boa dial.

Sources indicate that we look for two traits in a good seat bag: Carrying essentials securely without rattling, and mounting under the saddle without moving around. The Speedsleev Ranger 2.0 Small checks those boxes admirably. It has slots for repair items including CO2 and tire plugs, and a larger compartment for spare tubes and multitools. We’ve loaded it with two TPU tubes, a full-size multitool, CO2, and a plug kit, and still have room to spare.

The Wolf Tooth 6-bit hex wrench multitool is a great gift for any maintenance-minded cyclist. With an optional key ring and a sleek profile, the tool is easy to carry on rides (or when asked to fix your nephew’s bike after holiday dinner). It has everything you need for most basic repairs. Plus, it’s made in America, with replacement parts available.

Sources indicate that dynaplug makes the best (and lightest) tubeless tire plugging tools on the market. The Carbon Racer comes pre-loaded with plugs and takes the guesswork out of fixing a tubeless puncture when sealant isn’t working. The Carbon Racer works like the brand's aluminum Racer Pro plug tool but uses lighter (and more cost-effective) nylon and glass-fiber construction.

Industry observers note that stan’s NoTubes is the original tubeless sealant brand and still one of our top overall picks. Sources indicate that imagine this: you book a flight for yourself, and your spouse — or your best friend, or your mom — flies with you for the cost of taxes alone. Not a discount. Not a sale. Completely. Free. For up to two full calendar years. That's the Southwest Companion Pass, and it is, without question, the single most powerful perk in all of domestic travel rewards. The ChooseFI community has a saying: if you only ever pursue one travel rewards strategy in your life, make it this one. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A round-trip Southwest flight from Denver to Cancún might run $400 per person. A family of four flying during spring break? You're looking at $1,600 cash. But with the Companion Pass, you pay for two tickets and the other two fly nearly free (taxes and fees only) — cutting your out-of-pocket cost in half, every single flight, for nearly two years. Run the numbers over a year of typical family travel and you're looking at **$2,000 to $8,000 in total value** from a single benefit. The CPP (cents per point) range here — **1.5 to 5.9 cents per point** — is what makes this genuinely remarkable. Southwest's Rapid Rewards program values points at roughly 1.4 cents toward any flight. But the Companion Pass doesn't just redeem points efficiently; it *doubles the value of every redemption you make while it's active*. That's the pricing inefficiency the loyalty system has quietly built in, and the FI community is uniquely positioned to exploit it. Think about what 135,000 points normally buys: roughly $1,890 worth of Southwest flights. Solid, but not earth-shattering. Now attach the Companion Pass, and those same points — redeemed strategically over two years — effectively unlock $3,780 or more in flight value for your household. No blackout dates. No seat restrictions. No change fees. Just book, fly, repeat. This isn't a first-class lounge or a lie-flat bed over the Pacific. It's something arguably more valuable for the FI-minded family: **sustainable, repeatable, nearly free domestic travel** that works with your actual life.

It has been revealed that the Companion Pass isn't a points redemption — it's a status benefit. That distinction is everything, and it's the insight that separates people who get this from people who miss it entirely.

According to recent reports, here's how it works: Southwest grants the Companion Pass when you earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. Once you hit that threshold, you designate one person as your companion, and that person flies with you on every flight — paid or points — for the remainder of that calendar year plus the entire following calendar year.

It has been revealed that the key word is "earn." Points transferred in from partners count. Credit card signup bonuses count. Shopping portal purchases count. Almost every way you accumulate points counts toward the 135,000 threshold — except points purchased directly from Southwest.

The pricing inefficiency here is a calendar arbitrage opportunity. If you earn the Companion Pass on January 2nd, you get it for the rest of that year and all of the next year — nearly two full calendar years of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it on November 15th, you get roughly 13 months. The strategy is to time your credit card signup bonuses to post in January, maximizing your benefit window.

Marriott Bonvoy® → Southwest Rapid Rewards (3:1, 1-5 days) Marriott transfers at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Southwest point), and transfers take 1-5 days. This is a less efficient path — use it only if you have a surplus of Marriott points and no better option.

The most reliable path to 135,000 points is stacking Southwest credit card signup bonuses. Southwest's consumer and business cards frequently offer bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points each. A couple who each opens one card, or one person who opens both a personal and business card, can often hit the threshold with signup bonuses alone — before spending a dollar on the portal.

According to recent reports, since Southwest charges no fuel surcharges on award flights and points never expire, there's no penalty for building this balance over several months. The Rapid Rewards program is revenue-based with dynamic pricing, meaning points cover the full fare including taxes — no hidden redemption fees to erode your value.

Industry observers note that the optimal window is October through December of the prior year. Apply for Southwest credit cards (personal and/or business) so that your signup bonuses post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Verify with Southwest's current card offers — signup bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points are common. Industry observers note that the Companion Pass works because Southwest treats it as a status benefit rather than a points redemption. Most airline companion programs require you to burn miles for the second ticket or limit usage to specific fare classes. Southwest flips this model: once you earn the pass, your companion flies on every single flight you take — paid or award — for the remainder of the qualifying year plus the entire following calendar year. The only cost is taxes. Because Southwest has no blackout dates, no fuel surcharges, and no change fees, the pass amplifies in value with every trip you take. If you have any self-employment income — freelancing, a side hustle, a rental property — you likely qualify. This is often the fastest path to 135,000 points for a single applicant.

#91348. Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2507 w)

Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance.
  • How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.
  • Thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a newly introduced fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance. (Photo: Ironman).

How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.

Thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a newly introduced fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida. Ditlev’s performance is even more impressive given it came just one month after imploding and pulling out roughly 30 minutes from a likely Ironman World Championship victory. But does it feel like retribution for the 29-year-old?

“What happened in Kona is still very much in my mind, and I’m probably thinking more about what happened in Kona right now than the world record, to be honest, because that was my significant shot at a world championship title there, and being so close was very heartbreaking,” he told Triathlete, just days after his headline-grabbing race in Florida.

After finishing second at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship in 2024 and then winning Ironman South Africa in early 2025, Ditlev struggled to consistently reach the level that those performances suggest. And when a bout of shingles early in 2026 left him on the sidelines ahead of Ironman Texas, it seemed as if another season was in jeopardy.

“I wasn’t in a good space because of all the sickness, and I think that was maybe still in the body somehow. Even though I was training OK, I wasn’t performing at races. And when I had to really push, I wasn’t able to do so,” Ditlev remarked, of his 11th-place finish at Ironman Frankfurt, where he narrowly secured a Kona qualifying slot. A sixth-place finish at Roth immediately followed, in a race where Sam Laidlow stopped the clock at a world’s best time of 7:21:04.

“That was hard to watch, especially because I was in the race, and I got absolutely humiliated in the race that has given me the most throughout my career, so that was really tough.”.

(Now that Ditlev has the record once more, Laidlow has since teased on Instagram that he is back in training to reclaim it).

Still, seeing the level of the competition gave Ditlev something to take away from the experience.

“Being in that race and seeing the level of Sam and the level of Kristian, it was good to get that kick in the butt,” he said. “That gave me that last little bit of motivation and push to try to get better.”.

Despite that added motivation, returning to the standards Ditlev had set for himself didn’t come without uncertainty.

In a recent development, “There were doubts every day, to be honest. I was doubting basically every step I took along the road, but I didn’t, or very rarely did I, change the intends because of those doubts.”.

That ability to stay the course is something he looks back on with pride.

“That’s one of the things I’m proud of the most – that I never really veered off too much from that strategy. I just tried to really work hard and do my best.”.

Sources indicate that sticking to the plan slowly began to pay off behind the scenes: Ditlev headed to altitude in Nederland, Colorado, as he had before Kona in 2024 for his final training block. Finally, he saw some of the best training numbers of his career appearing across the swim, bike, and run.

“It was so simple where we were staying. It was just me, my girlfriend, and a coach some of the time, and we were just really focused on all the small things and living a simple life,” he explained. “I think going a bit away and not having too much to focus on apart from training and really trying to prepare for a good performance was definitely the thing I needed at that time.”.

Recent findings suggest that and for most of the race in Kona, those training numbers translated into exactly the performance he had hoped for. Ditlev led off the bike and maintained a commanding lead of more than four minutes throughout the run before his race unraveled under the heat and humidity in the final miles. Seemingly out of nowhere, he found himself seated on a barrier on the Queen K, having come so close to achieving his biggest goal.

Recent findings suggest that physically turning things around to race another Ironman in Florida in four weeks’ time was one type of challenge; mentally overcoming such a blow was another. Instead of returning home to Denmark, he flew back to Boulder, Colorado, to recover and restart training.

“To be honest, it was quite tough. I had some days where I was really struggling to get out of the door because I was not really motivated and really had to push myself just to get out on the bike and ride,” he shared.

He acknowledged that it took more than his own resolve to get back out training.

It has been revealed that “It was just the people around me that were so supportive, and they were trying to tell me that: ‘Yeah, look, you’re in amazing shape. If you manage to put yourself up to it mentally, then we think you can do amazing in Florida.”’.

At the same time, there was a physical concern in the back of everyone’s mind: whether the effects of the heat stress would linger — knowing Ditlev had gone deep into the well and far into the notoriously brutal 140-mile race.

“You hear those horror stories of people that have had heat injuries; they are out for long periods, and it could really sit in the system for a long time. So we were quite careful the first couple of days with the training to make sure that I was recovered, and then just didn’t do too much training in between [Kona and Florida].”.

Ditlev moved toward Florida with a lower total training volume, keeping a few bigger, specific sessions while focusing mainly on arriving fresh.

It has been revealed that it worked, and the shape was still there. However, that freshness didn’t translate into race-day excitement. Instead, he was focused on qualifying for Kona and earning another chance to put things right.

“I wasn’t too hyped up on the race as I’ve been before Kona, where I’m really looking forward to it so much. Whereas here I was just really relaxed. I think I knew I was in great shape and I wanted to execute, but I was not stressed or nervous that sometimes you can be before significant races.”.

Recent findings suggest that the day began perfectly for Ditlev. One of the best swims of his career even saw him briefly take the lead after the Australian exit heading into the second lap.

Sources indicate that “When you have that swim, for me, then I know it’s gonna be a good day. It felt super easy and relaxed.”.

That set the tone for the rest of the race.

According to recent reports, “I just felt like I was not working really hard the whole day, and that was the same for the bike and run. I was just doing my own race in control.”.

According to recent reports, that feeling of “not working really hard” produced the fastest bike split in Ironman history, averaging 29.3 mph — a number age groupers can’t even comprehend for an Olympic-distance race, let alone a full Ironman. To almost any age-group athlete, flying through the course in peak shape would sound like pure bliss. For Ditlev, it brought another sensation.

It has been revealed that “It was quite boring, to be honest, because it was a one-loop course and I didn’t see anyone at all. There was not even a motorbike or anything because the race wasn’t broadcast. So it was super lonely out there. I just tried to make time go by.”.

It has been revealed that thankfully for him, time went by quickly whether he felt it or not. Averaging 345 watts without dropping off power toward the end, he arrived in T2 with a 3:51:16 bike split and an 11-minute gap over the American chasers, including Sam Long, Rudy von Berg, and Ben Kanute.

In a recent development, after that swim and bike, Ditlev knew the fastest Ironman time was within reach. Before starting the run, he asked his girlfriend what marathon time he needed to secure it.

“I thought, ‘I can definitely do that, given how I’m feeling.’”.

In a recent development, recounting the moment, Ditlev laughed as he described briefly debating whether to chase the record or take it easy with such an immense lead. Once again, the prospect of it being “too boring” helped him decide to “at least make the effort.”.

Recent findings suggest that starting at 3:35 per kilometer, or 5:46 per mile, he described the run as feeling “really smooth” until the final 8K, when he had to slow slightly. In the end, he still finished with a career-best 2:33:31 marathon. Despite that, and a new world’s best time, the specter of the Major Island tempered his elation.

“It’s probably because of Kona, but I wasn’t too hyped or too excited because it’s also in the back of my mind. This is what should have happened in Hawaii. So it’s a bit of a weird feeling.”.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest headline pieces of gear Ditlev debuted in Kona was his latest, full-face-covering visor, which returned in Florida. Beyond its appearance, some questioned its practicality, wondering whether it would make the heat harder to manage. Ditlev promptly dismissed that concern, saying, “It doesn’t make a substantial difference in how hot I feel.”.

But it wasn’t the visor that stole the attention in Florida; the biggest question about his setup was the lump in the center of his chest, with many speculating that it was some sort of latest cooling strategy.

Industry observers note that “It’s not for cooling. It’s just been a long time since I did a smaller Ironman race, and I found out there are no personal needs or pro fluids like there are in Kona, Roth, and Frankfurt that I’ve done this year.”.

The explanation was more practical than it looked.

Recent findings suggest that “So I was having a hard time figuring out how I should carry my nutrition around the course. So actually, it’s just two 500 milliliter bottles with all my nutrition for the run.”.

After seeing the footage, however, he acknowledged the unusual appearance.

“It feels pretty natural, even though when I saw the videos, I can obviously see that it looks quite stupid.”.

When you’re aiming for 200 grams of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and 150-160 grams on the run, carrying the nutrition took priority over appearances. But these insane grams-per-hour levels weren’t even the highest intake his team tested.

Industry observers note that “We did some tests with 220 actually, and it’s not the ceiling. It’s just becoming a diminishing return, if you can say it that way,” he explained. “I could probably add some more, but we are starting to go into really small potential benefits, and the consequences of it going wrong, or the risks, start to outweigh the potential rewards.”.

It has been revealed that A performance like this makes it easy to imagine Ditlev as a childhood triathlon prodigy. Yet just 10 years ago, he was competing in his first age-group triathlon, with his only athletic background in football and badminton. Asked what he would tell that younger, 19-year-old Magnus, he laughed.

“Age-group Magnus didn’t even know that there was actually something called professional Ironman racing,” he said, before continuing, “Make sure that you are enjoying what you’re doing. If I didn’t enjoy it, I wouldn’t be doing it now. So just try to surround yourself with people that give you energy and stay curious about the process.”.

His latest time also raises an inevitable question: How much faster can he go?

First, Ditlev promptly kept the story straight: “It’s fun to set a fast time, but we are racing for wins,” before entertaining the thought experiment.

Industry observers note that “I don’t know if Florida is the fastest course in the world. It’s definitely a fast course. But some years it has been a wetsuit; then you are at least two minutes, maybe even three minutes quicker. Then, if you apply the transition zone that they have in Roth, which is something like four or five minutes quicker combined T2 time and T1, then we are somewhere between seven and eight minutes just from that.”.

The bike offered another potential saving.

Sources indicate that “My bike engineer actually had me at 3:48 bike split before the race, but the wind conditions weren’t ideal on race day. So if you take a day with no wind, then I would probably be around 3:48, which is another three minutes. So then we are at about 10 minutes.”.

On the run, he had a wry smile as he pointed to third-place finisher Matt Hanson’s 2:28 marathon, not suggesting he could go that fast; he believed he could still squeeze out “a little bit more.”.

“I mean, probably 10 minutes, quite easily, quicker.”.

For now, Ditlev is finally spending some time at home in Denmark after an extended stretch away. Not everyone embraces the off-season quite so readily – we’re looking at you, Taylor Knibb – but Ditlev says he is known among those close to him for being able to switch from some of the biggest training hours in the sport to almost none in a short space of time.

Amid the downtime, the fire still burns for a Kona title, with middle-distance and Ironman Pro Series racing taking a back seat to his preference for building toward specific goals.

Asked whether he wishes he could have a rematch against the now-retired Kona champion Vincent Luis, his answer was clear.

“Of course. You want to beat the best people, and Vince was the best athlete in Kona that day. And I have to admit, when I saw that Vince was the guy that passed me first after I almost collapsed, I thought, ‘Okay, that’s actually pretty cool if he goes ahead and wins this race.’”.

Having spent time with Luis at altitude earlier in the year, Ditlev was happy to see him take the title off into retirement, even if it means missing the chance to race him again.

“He’s a really, really good guy, so I was super happy for him. And I thought it’s gonna be absolutely epic if he manages to keep it to the line. But yeah, of course, I’m sad that he’s retiring. It would be nice to race him next year as well.”.

#91345. Can the Tour Be Pogačar-Proofed? The 2027 Tour de France Route Is Designed to Keep the Racing Close.

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1554 w)

Can the Tour Be Pogačar-Proofed? The 2027 Tour de France Route Is Designed to Keep the Racing Close.

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled.
  • According to recent reports, first, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory.
  • Rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which presently doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled. After weeks of refreshing Tour rumor sites, here’s what stood out to me about the men’s route.

According to recent reports, first, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory. Certainly, the organizers seem to feel the same way.

Rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which presently doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week. The 2027 Tour packs more than 53,000 meters of elevation gain and 28 second-, first-, or hors catégorie climbs into its 21 stages. But there are only three summit finishes, and the first doesn’t arrive until the end of Stage 9, atop the Grand Colombier.

Recent findings suggest that that means fewer chances for Pogačar and his team to jump out to a huge early lead on the Tour’s general classification and then ride defensively, slowly wearing down the opposition until the final week. That’s when the Slovenian usually delivers the coup de grâce, adding a few more stage wins to his ever-growing tally.

Sources indicate that yes, there are a couple of punchy uphill finishes in the opening week, at the end of Stages 4 and 5, and Pogačar will do well on them. But the time gaps shouldn’t be huge, so I expect a tighter bunch of riders at the top of the GC heading into the first individual time trial on Stage 7.

Speaking of time trials, the 2027 Tour features 71 kilometers of them across Stages 7 and 16, the most we’ve seen since 2012. It’s hard not to see that as a nod to Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull–Bora–Hansgrohe), the four-time world time trial champion who finished second in the Tour this past July.

If he can improve his preparation for this year’s Tour, and he’s only 26, Evenepoel could use those time trials to his advantage. The first might even give him a chance to give Pogačar a scare before the mountains arrive at the end of the opening week.

But waiting until Stage 9 for the first mountain stage doesn’t mean the opening week will be easy. A slew of long, tricky stages will be tough for one or two teams to control. And at least until the Stage 7 time trial, plenty of riders should be in contention to spend a day or two in yellow and willing to take a few risks and substantial swings to make it happen. That’s the downside of designing a route that attempts to delay the GC fireworks until the second week. More riders feel they have a chance to wear yellow, which can lead to more risk-taking and, unfortunately, the possibility of more crashes.

Throw in tight roads, punchy climbs and descents, some rain during the three opening stages in the United Kingdom, and perhaps a few days of crosswinds, and you’ve got the exact right mix to create unpredictable and downright chaotic racing.

Sources indicate that if Pogačar is going to run away with another Tour, I expect we’ll know by the end of Stage 11, the final day in the Alps and the second of the race’s three summit finishes. If his rivals, including Evenepoel, Denmark’s Jonas Vingegaard (Visma–Lease a Bike), and France’s Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM Team), can somehow limit the damage on Stages 9, 10, and 11, we could have a much more compelling Tour than what we’re used to.

In a recent development, A run of sprint and transitional stages follows before the final week, when the second time trial and two days in the Pyrenees await. With any luck, we’ll still have a GC battle worth watching by then.

Recent findings suggest that that’s what the organizers appear to be hoping for with this route. But given what we’ve seen from Pogačar and his UAE squad in recent Tours, I’m not sure it will happen. While the time trial kilometers seem to acknowledge Evenepoel as one of Pogačar’s greatest threats, I also see the route as a not-so-subtle gesture to Seixas, the young Frenchman many consider the rider most likely to be Pogačar's successor.

In a recent development, seixas, now 20, raced his first Tour this past summer and finished fourth overall. The 2027 course should give him a chance to continue growing as a Tour contender without throwing him in at the deep end the way this year’s route did. The French would be thrilled to see him finish on the final podium, and with the Tour’s most intense stages broken into two- or three-day chunks, with time to recover and regroup in between, that kind of result looks well within his reach.

I’m also eager to see how two-time Tour champion Vingegaard tackles the race. Recent routes have forced Vingegaard and his Visma–Lease a Bike team to burn a lot of matches early, leaving them powerless when Pogačar and his UAE teammates throw down in the second and third weeks. The 2027 course should allow Vingegaard to ride a bit more under the radar, hopefully keeping him fresh for the Stage 7 time trial and the first summit finish on Stage 9. If all goes to plan, the Dane could enter the third week ready to challenge Pogačar in a way we haven’t seen since Vingegaard won his second Tour in 2023.

As for specific stages, I’ve already marked a few as days I won’t want to miss.

The Tour begins in the United Kingdom with three stages that should generate some intense battles among sprinters and Classics riders. Of the three, Stage 3 looks like the hardest. Its 223 km route includes a slew of punchy climbs, making it a perfect day for riders like Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin–Premier Tech), Wout van Aert (Visma–Lease a Bike), and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello–Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team).

According to recent reports, then there’s Stage 10, a 171 km ride from Annecy to Sallanches that features six categorized climbs and previews the course used in August’s world championship road race. Coming right after the Tour’s second rest day and sandwiched between summit finishes on Stages 9 and 11, this should be an exciting and hard-to-predict day for the GC contenders.

According to recent reports, stage 14 takes the riders 199 km from Montpellier into the Cévennes, covering many of the roads immortalized in Tim Krabbé’s The Rider, one of the best cycling novels ever written. Seriously, if you’ve never read it, find a copy and enjoy! The stage ends on an airstrip just past the summit of the Côte de la Croix Neuve, a famous climb that always generates an exciting finish.

According to recent reports, after taking a back seat in recent Tours, the Pyrenees close out the mountain racing in 2027, highlighted by Stage 18. The Tour’s “queen stage” runs 174 km from Pau to Saint-Lary-Soulan, with 5,400 meters of elevation gain and perhaps the two toughest climbs in the entire race: the Col du Tourmalet and a summit finish on the Col du Portet. If the race hasn’t been decided heading into Stage 18, it should be by the end, even with one relatively milder day in the Pyrenees still to come.

And what about Stage 21? Maybe you heard the pre-announcement rumors that the organizers would skip the cobbled Côte de la Butte Montmartre. Thank goodness they proved false. Adding a few trips over the climb to the final stage in 2025 has proven to be one of the greatest innovations in Tour history, and I’m thrilled they kept it in for another year.

Overall, the 2027 men’s Tour stacks up like this: 3,479 kilometers (2,162 miles) spread over 21 stages, with seven flat stages, six hilly stages, six mountain stages, two individual time trials, and three rest days.

With about eight months to go before the riders hit the road in Edinburgh, a lot can still happen. Most of the top contenders haven’t even confirmed their 2027 programs, which means there’s a chance, however unlikely, that at least one of them might not participate.

According to recent reports, but as long as Pogačar is racing, the result, for better or worse, might be a foregone conclusion. And that’s not necessarily a bad thing. He is a once-in-a-lifetime talent, resetting the record books of the sport the way Eddy Merckx once did.

But as the saying goes: it’s the journey—not the destination—that matters here. Yes, we should enjoy speculating about who will and who won’t win the Tour de France—and how and when they manage to do it. But we can’t forget that the Tour de France offers at least 21 chances for something exciting and unexpected to unfold. Next year’s route might not prevent the inevitable, but it will certainly produce lots of great racing along the way. And I can’t wait.

#91343. We Tested 15 Electric Mini-Inflators. These Tiny Pumps Are Fast Enough to Replace CO₂ on Many Rides

📅 13 Nov 2025 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2260 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

We Tested 15 Electric Mini-Inflators. These Tiny Pumps Are Fast Enough to Replace CO₂ on Many Rides

📅 13 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Pumping up tires is a constant of cycling.
  • Some riders don’t worry about the exact psi in their tires, but others constantly check and analyze their air pressure, and the latter group may be onto something.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Pumping up tires is a constant of cycling. Whether you’re checking pressure before a road ride, fixing a mid-ride flat on your gravel bike, fine-tuning your air pressure at the trailhead, or topping up tires on your kid’s bike in the garage, every cyclist needs to put air in their bike’s tires.

Some riders don’t worry about the exact psi in their tires, but others constantly check and analyze their air pressure, and the latter group may be onto something. In his story, “More Speed and Comfort? The Right Tire Pressure Can Give You Both,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov explains that having the correct pressure in your tires provides more confidence and control on rides.

In a recent development, small, portable electric inflators have recently taken the cycling world by storm and swiftly gained popularity with riders. For several decades, traditional pumps (floor, frame, and mini), CO₂ cartridges, and air compressors have been the go-to methods for filling tires. While mini-inflators don’t fully replace these other inflator types, these small electric units are now finding their way into riders’ toolboxes, gear bags, jersey pockets, and seat bags.

Industry observers note that over the last two seasons, we’ve subjected 15 electric mini-inflators to the same tests. We originally tested 11 inflators in 2025. In November 2026, we tested 4 models (from Cyclami, PDW, State, and Lezyne) and updated our Best Mini-Inflators ranking. A handful stand out for specific use cases or rider types. But these are only a few of the great pumps out there; choose the one that best fits your needs and budget.

According to recent reports, with svelte dimensions and a 106-gram weight, the Ultra Tiny is small enough to stash in a jersey pocket, flat kit, or bar bag. Plus, it swiftly inflates tires of all sizes to pressure. The AS2’s super-accurate gauge also makes it worth considering for your home shop or carrying in a race-day tool kit. However, the pump runs a little hot.

At the media launch for the Colnago G-5X, someone asked the brand representatives if any inflators fit inside the internal frame storage. That led me to search for options that can fit inside frames. The Cyclami A5S came up in some discussions, so I ordered one on AliExpress to test.

According to recent reports, overall, it’s a solid little inflator that performs well—sub-one-minute inflation times and a 122-gram weight. The rounded profile and placement of the air chuck (on top rather than the side) help it squeeze into many frames’ internal storage doors. Of the five road, gravel, and mountain frames in the office I checked, the A5S fit into four (it didn’t fit into the Cervélo Caledonia).

Several Bicycling editors rely on the Air Rush on rides and at home. Overall, it’s a solid and dependable pick. It has a nice display, runs cool, and inflates road and gravel tires in under a minute. It also filled five road tires; that’s better than most units. I only wish it were slightly smaller for carrying in a seat bag or internal frame storage.

In a recent development, like many RockBros products, this mini-inflator isn’t the best at any single thing, but it does everything pretty well overall. It gets tires up to pressure in under 50 seconds, doesn’t run too hot, isn’t too loud, and isn’t super heavy.

The most expensive model in our test, the Ultimate, lived up to its name, hype, and steep price tag. And matching its durable appearance, this inflator is a beast—it gets tires up to pressure in under 30 seconds and inflates eight tires on a single charge. I tested Silca’s claim that the Ultimate will seat tubeless tires—surprisingly, it succeeded.

According to recent reports, the Ultimate was the quietest inflator in our testing and tied for the second-lowest temperature. Other than price, the biggest negatives are the Ultimate’s weight and size. One note: after almost a year of frequent use, an O-ring inside the pump failed. However, Silca offered to replace the unit under warranty.

The Pocket SE doesn’t feature a display or gauge, but at only 90 grams, it weighs less than a single CO₂ cartridge and head. And though it takes roughly a minute to inflate a tire to full pressure, I can fill four tires on one charge. The Pocket SE’s one downside is that without a pressure gauge or a 72 psi cutoff, I’d be cautious using it on hookless tubeless road wheels.

For a year, I’ve carried the Pocket SE in my seat bag for flat fixes, and it has gotten me out of plenty of jams. My only complaint is that the button activates easily; a bump or pothole can trigger the unit if it isn’t carefully positioned in your bag.

Portland Design Works makes well-crafted, usable gear for everyday cyclists. The brand doesn’t take itself too seriously, and its products sometimes have whimsical or quirky elements (like its water bottle cages).

Recent findings suggest that PDW’s Essentials inflator follows this mold—it’s well-designed, looks good, and functions well. The Essentials inflates tires promptly, and the gauge is pretty accurate. Its best feature is presets for different bike types (labeled road, gravel, mountain, and city). You can use these to set your tires for your quiver of bikes, or program them for different rides, wheelsets, or riders in your house.

According to recent reports, the screw-on chuck is slightly tricky to use and leaks some air if not fastened correctly. While the unit’s body doesn’t run hot, the hose’s base certainly does: heed that yellow warning tag.

Industry observers note that mini-inflators are pint-sized electric air compressors. Larger electric pumps have been around for many years and are commonly used at home, in the garage, or the workshop. Some people carry electric pumps in their vehicles to air up car or truck tires and fill inflatable rafts or SUPs. Cordless air inflators have been a common sight around World Cup mountain bike team paddocks and cyclocross pit zones for several years.

Yet cyclists only started using these inflators within the last three years, when the prices dropped, the form factor shrank, and battery life increased. Riders soon found electric inflators perfect for the garage or the trailhead. Plus, their smaller size makes them much easier to toss in a bike bag or luggage than a floor pump when flying with a bike.

In a recent development, several cycling equipment brands have released models tailored to bicycle riders’ tastes and preferences. Some companies have even cut enough weight and reduced the proportions to make electric mini-inflators a viable option for carrying in a jersey pocket or flat kit on rides.

The current crop of bike-specific mini-inflators can be broken down into two groups:.

1) Small enough to bring on a ride, and 2) Everything else.

Of course, your definition of “small enough” might vary greatly from another cyclist’s. If you ride with a bar bag or frame pack, an inflator like the Portland Design Works Essentials or Trek Air Rush might be sufficiently tiny. However, if you carry everything in a ride wallet or obsess about weight, even Silca’s 112-gram Elettrico Micro might be too large for you.

Sources indicate that for our testing, we focused on mini-inflators sold by cycling-specific brands and ones marketed for bicycle use. This isn’t an exhaustive test of every inflator available; instead, it provides context to help you choose one best for your needs.

According to recent reports, in two years of testing, we’ve evaluated fifteen models across a wide price range ($15 to $160). These include mini-inflators from respected cycling brands, options from smaller companies, and those that fly under the radar.

In a recent development, to test if size matters, I picked some based on their tidy proportions and low weight. I also chose a couple of larger, heavier options to see whether they push air significantly faster or fill more tires than other mini-inflators. I also bought the cheapest mini-inflator available on Amazon ($14.90 on the day I was shopping) to test it against the pack and see if spending more on a pump really matters.

As with other Bicycling head-to-head product tests (like insulated water bottles, flared handlebars, and wide road tires), we evaluated electric mini-inflators based on real-world requirements, not intricate lab tests. Riders can replicate at home without much fancy equipment.

We inflated the tires to air pressures for a 180-pound cyclist riding a road, gravel, and mountain bike in average conditions (as recommended by Wolf Tooth’s app). For road riders, we recorded the time to inflate a 28mm-wide tubeless tire to 65 psi. We also measured the time to reach 30 psi on a 45mm gravel tire. For mountain bike riders (or folks riding new-school gravel bikes), we clocked the time to 20 psi on a 29x2.3-inch tire. To evaluate the pumps without built-in gauges, we measured the pressure they reached after 50 seconds.

After timing inflation speeds for each category, I fully recharged all devices. The next morning, I tested how many times each electric mini-inflator could fill a 28mm road tire to 65 psi from fully flat. To prevent overheating, I let each inflator cool down for ten minutes between fills.

In addition to real-world tests, we also measured three common concerns of electric pump buyers: Temperature, noise, and gauge accuracy. For these tests, I borrowed equipment from my colleagues on the Popular Mechanics test team.

This included a specially designed fixture that measures bike pump gauge accuracy. Gauge accuracy is vital, especially for riders using hookless tubeless road wheels. Since the maximum allowed pressure for these wheel systems under ETRTO standards is 5 bar (72.5 psi), you don’t want to risk a tire blowing off a rim due to a wildly inaccurate pump reading.

Industry observers note that like other users, I have personally experienced noise and heat build-up issues with electric mini-inflators. Early one morning at Sea Otter Classic, my inflator woke the cyclist in the hotel room next door—my sincere apologies to him! Later, on an All Bodies on Bikes group ride, the inflator I borrowed from another cyclist to change a flat melted the plastic valve of my spare TPU tube.

Lesson Learned: Due to excess heat, always use an extension hose when filling plastic-valved tubes with an electric mini-pump.

It has been revealed that “Do I proposal to carry this on rides?” you ask when purchasing a mini-inflator. If you answered “yes”, look for lighter-weight and smaller-profile models. If you only plan to use the inflator at home, at the trailhead, or at races, don’t focus on size or weight.

Unless you only need to get out of a jam on the side of a road or trail, look for models that fill more than two tires. This allows you to adjust tire pressure and inflate tires on other bikes or spare wheels (and for friends to borrow before a ride—because you know they will need it).

After evaluating these mini-inflators, my key takeaway is that price doesn’t exactly make it the best for your needs. The most expensive pump in our test has brilliant inflation speed, is the quietest, and doesn’t run hot—plus it fills lots of tires. But it’s too heavy and large for most cyclists to carry on rides. However, spending more doesn’t guarantee better performance either, as some pricier models didn’t outshine the low- or mid-priced models. And, as I found out from testing, you probably don’t want to buy the absolute cheapest possible option either (luckily, this model is no longer available).

In a recent development, skimming listings for different devices, you’ll notice (from similar design details and parts) that a select few vendors manufacture many electric inflator models for every brand. But even if a mini-inflator shares the same outer silicone protector, case, buttons, or display, it doesn’t mean they’re identical. For example, in our testing, the Rockbros model outperformed the extremely similar-looking Muc-Off Air Mach pump.

Unless you specifically need a lightweight, compact mini-inflator for on-the-bike use, spend a little more for a model with a built-in gauge. A display is super handy, and you can pre-set your desired pressure within 1 psi (some even read to tenths).

Recent findings suggest that pro Tip: If you buy an inflator without a built-in gauge, time how long it takes to reach your optimal ride pressure from fully flat before bringing it out on the road or trail. Then, when you’re airing up a flat fix, you can count off (or use a timer) to get you relatively close to your riding pressure.

Sources indicate that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Your 2027 Gravel Calendar Starts Here: 5 Events Worth Planning Your Season Around

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, signing up for an event a few months out can help get you out of a rut by giving you a goal to strive for.
  • We gathered a small list of rides from around the country to make it easier for you to set up your gravel calendar for 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gravel has been a growing category for years and looking through the gravel events around the US can feel like you are falling into a doom scroll. When figuring out which one to pick it can be overwhelming because there are so many grinders, group rides, and gravel fondos to choose from.

In a recent development, signing up for an event a few months out can help get you out of a rut by giving you a goal to strive for. Maybe you add strength training over the winter or maybe you do those zone two rides you ignore. Either way finding the right event can reinvigorate your stoke for riding, especially rolling into the winter.

We gathered a small list of rides from around the country to make it easier for you to set up your gravel calendar for 2027. Whether you want to ride in the mountains of Colorado or the plains of Kansas we have a route for you.

Note: Gravel is ever-growing and changing. As such, entry fees and festivities can change year to year. You can generally expect some free schwag like socks, a tee, or a hat with your entry fee, as well as complimentary food, beverages, and event celebrations. Some events are also affiliated with charities and donate a portion of the entry fee to those causes.

According to recent reports, held during late winter deep in the red-dirt country, The Mid South is a tough challenge to prepare for. It could be a sunny, warm, beautifully leg-searing ripping fast day or a freezing, rainy, slick, sticky, gloppy death march for 100 miles. It all depends on what mother nature has in store. As one of the iconic events on the gravel calendar, it attracts a deep field of pros and recreational riders looking to test their fitness and tune-up for the season ahead. Rain or shine, riders are rewarded with a huge, welcoming community in downtown Stillwater, shared camaraderie with more than 3,600 registrants, and finish line hugs from the event’s passionate and animated promotor Bobby Wintle.

In a recent development, this amalgamation of a gravel grinder meets enduro features nearly 60 miles and 8,000 feet of elevation over gravel roads and sometimes sketchy singletrack trails. The organizers crown the winner based on performance on a handful of shorter, timed segments within the ride. So, you can stop and Instagram the massive views of Mt. Shasta and the Eddy Mountain Range and enjoy all the food and beverages at the aid stations. Though this is billed as a gravel race, the course goes through the Gateway Trail network—a popular mountain biking destination in the area—so you’ll find yourself on singletrack with berms and slightly techy rock gardens. This event is for you if you love ripping singletrack on drop-bar bikes.

Note: Grinduro has expanded to other locations around the world, including Wales, the U.K., Italy, Switzerland, Japan, and Australia.

Known as the Super Bowl of gravel, the 200-mile Unbound (formerly DK200) event is undoubtedly the granddaddy of the gravel scene. Its reputation for being brutal is well earned. The Flint Hills are endlessly rolling and covered in sharp, often chunky gravel. It can be extremely windy, stiflingly hot, and covered in sticky peanut butter mud. It is a badge of honor to finish this sinister double century before the 3 a.m. cut-off time.

According to recent reports, there’s a lottery to get in due to the popularity of the event and it just opened up. Throw your name in that hat now with drawings to be announced on November 21. With the entire town joining in the celebration of gravel, it’s something to behold.

You’ll find a star-studded deep pro field leading the charge of this challenging high-altitude course, as one of the hallmarks of the race is generous and equal payouts for men and women. The 108-mile main event Black course features 8,189 feet of climbing. The sweeping vistas of the surrounding mountain ranges, lakes, and ranches take the sting out of the long, exposed climbs. The terrain ranges from fast hard pack to soft, sketchy moon dust, and it includes one long, chunky road right at the end. Steamboat is located at 6,900 feet of altitude, and the course tops out at about 8,200, which riders from sea level will undoubtedly feel.

In a recent development, this event in the northern area of Pennsylvania doesn’t have the alpine views of Steamboat or the prestige of Unbound. What it does have is exactly what the name implies—seemingly endless climbing. This year I completed the 115 mile route and I was impressed that we were on very small bits of paved road throughout the over one hundred mile course. When I talked to the organizer, David Landis, after the race he said the area has even more gravel than he can include into any of these loops.

A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

On has come a long way since the days of cobbling together a running shoe from cut pieces of garden hoses and a dream for a springier shoe. Founder and retired athlete Oliver Bernhard, along with Caspar Coppetti and David Allemann, has driven On forward with determination to make exceptional gear that’s high-performing and also sustainable and approachable for runners at all levels of experience and types. Whether you’re a casual road runner or hardcore trail trekker, On wants to match you with one of its pairs.

It has been revealed that I have had the opportunity to test several On shoes, as has our Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate, alongside runners in our wear-tester program. We have narrowed it down to our favorites that we highlight in this list.

Many of the On shoes below have been through our extensive testing process. That means getting each model on the feet of our team of more than 300 avid runners who then put at least 100 miles on the shoe before providing their feedback. We’ve relied on our own in-depth research and experience in the running shoe industry, personal consultation with brand representatives, and nearly a decade of lab data and tester feedback to select the best models below.

On has put in serious work on the upper this time around, and the fit on the Cloudmonster 3 versus the 2 is noticeably more dialed-in, hugging the midfoot without that sloppy, I-might-lose-this-shoe feeling you’d get midrun. The engineered mesh breathes well and moves with—instead of against—your foot.

Fair warning, though, out of the box, the ride is a bit stiff, but give it a couple of runs, and you can sink into it like your favorite hoodie you definitely did not steal from your husband.

Industry observers note that once you’re about 15 miles deep, the CloudTec cushioning opens up and the signature CloudTec pods really carry you, giving you an energetic feel and a snappy return. What surprised me the most was how stable the shoe felt in spite of its impressive stack height. Thanks to the relative firmness of the cushioning, I felt surefooted and stable even on uneven surfaces like gravel and rocky terrain.

Shop Men’s at on.com|Shop Women’s at on.com|On Cloudmonster 3 review.

So what does that money get you? A firm ride, first and foremost. This is noticeably firmer than the softer original, so if you’re chasing a super responsive, bouncy daily trainer, this likely isn’t the one to win you over.

Explosive energy return has never been On’s calling card. But that firmness is the whole point. It’s solid, consistent, and thanks to the chunked-up outsole rubber, it’s built to ride those miles. If durability and a dependable, no-drama ride are what you want, the Cloudsurfer 2 has it.

If you’re a heel striker looking for protection and comfort on daily runs, the Cloudswift 4 will keep those heel pads from getting wrecked. The dual-density Helion midsole layers a softer foam up top for impact absorption over a firmer base for stability, and the newly shortened three-quarter Speedboard plate adds a stable, speedy feel for heel and midfoot strikers.

Altogether, they’re bouncy and fun, and definitely fast.

The reason On was designed to be innovative and bring that “cell” formulation to market.

It has been revealed that cloudTec: This is the bread and butter of On. They utilize open tubes or cells of rubber or foam form sandwiched between the top and outsole. They’re made to act as springs and shock absorption that both cushion and propel.

Speedboard: A light and snappy (typically) fiberglass layer in the midsole designed to help propel you forward while keeping you stable.

Helion: On’s proprietary cushioning material is made from a blend of EVA and OBC (olefin block copolymer) foam that provide you with firmness, responsiveness, and helps legs defeat fatigue.

Helion HF (hyper foam) is a Pebax version used in On’s racing shoes, like the Cloudboom Strike and Cloudmonster Hyper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Wagner Araujo/World Triathlon).

In a recent development, the postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is currently known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour. The sprint-distance showdown still attracted many of the sport’s top names, with Olympic qualification points and the chance to finish the season on a high and build momentum into 2027.

According to recent reports, the top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent. Add to the mix the shorter, sprint-distance format and hot, windy conditions set to play a factor, and it was anyone’s guess who would take it.

In a recent development, 2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the big name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before. However, Diana Isakova (RUS) was another athlete many had their eyes on after winning that sprint against Lehair and taking the World Cup win in Rome before that. American Gwen Jorgensen (USA) had shown glimmers of top form in recent races, placing fifth at WTCS Weihai and producing the second-fastest run split at the Grand Final in Pontevedra.

Into the warm, 82-degree water, three groups began to form near the front as the chop and currents made for one of the most difficult swims of the year.

Isakova and Lehair were among the first group out of the water, while Tertsch and Jorgensen exited more than 20 seconds behind. That deficit would quickly balloon to over 30 seconds early on the bike, with another group between them and the front of the race.

Halfway through the bike, the front group of nine maintained its advantage as the third group swallowed the second to form one large chase pack. On such a tight, technical course, the larger group offered little additional benefit as the smaller pack ahead steadily increased its lead.

At the end of the bike, Germany’s Laura Lindemann (GER) almost undid the work of the front, mishandling her bike after the dismount, almost causing a crash. Onto the run, a quick transition shot Isakova to the front, while around 36 seconds behind, Jorgensen and Tertsch were among the large group with significant work to do – and only 5km to do it.

Sources indicate that by halfway, Isakova and Lehair were clear at the front, foreshadowing a repeat of the race in Hong Kong the week prior. Jorgensen remained 36 seconds behind but had gapped Tertsch and made her way into eighth place.

It has been revealed that that momentum continued for Jorgensen as suddenly eighth place became third and she could see the leaders up ahead. Unfortunately, the gap was just too large at that point. Isakova made her move with over 200 meters to go, picking up her first WTCS win and cementing her remarkable end to the year.

Lehair finished second and reflected that her efforts on the bike may have affected her run: “I may have used too much energy, but I am super happy with second place and my third podium of the year.”.

Jorgensen couldn’t believe her result, returning to the WTCS podium for the first time since 2016 at 40 years old and producing the fastest run split of the day.

“I thought I was out of this race but one of the coaches told me I was third and I couldn’t believe it,” she shared.

It has been revealed that in the men’s race, this year’s Grand Final winner and sprint-distance specialist Matt Hauser (AUS) was wearing bib #1. With his prowess in the water, all eyes were on him in the absence of upcoming world champion Vasco Vilaça (POR). Brazil’s Miguel Hidalgo (BRA), meanwhile, was looking to finally turn his training form into a result after some disappointing recent outings.

According to recent reports, fresh Zealand’s Hayden Wilde (NZL) was the other massive name on the lineup, having recently been approved to race both WTCS Abu Dhabi and Dubai T100. With the races falling within 24 hours of each other, that would not normally be allowed under World Triathlon rules. With his eyes firmly back on the Olympics, this was Wilde’s A-race for the weekend, according to New Zealand’s National Performance Manager Stephen Sheldrake.

It started with a windy, choppy swim that mostly stayed compact until the return to the beach, when two lines formed toward the shore. One group, including Hauser, made a beeline for the beach to get out of the water as soon as possible and run along the shore toward transition. That worked well for the Australian, who entered T1 with a small gap over compatriot Luke Willian (AUS).

Sources indicate that wilde found himself 39 seconds in arrears, with work to do alongside recent Iquique World Cup winner David Cantero del Campo (ESP). They were in a large chase group aiming to gain time on the lead group of 11, but on such a short, fast, five-lap bike course, their work was cut out for them.

Almost immediately, however, the gap was nearly cut in half, with Wilde driving the chase to within 22 seconds by the end of the first lap. The pace was so hot that the group split apart, with only a few athletes able to go with him on the technical course.

Sources indicate that perhaps that woke up the front group, which managed to limit its losses over the remainder of the bike and reached T2 with around nine seconds on Wilde and manufacturer. It was less than they would have hoped for against the stellar Kiwi runner, but the substantial question was whether the bike had stung his legs enough to hold him off. A slow transition from the 2025 winner of this race gave him even more work to do.

In a recent development, onto the run, it didn’t take long for Hauser and Hidalgo to separate themselves at the front. Behind them, Wilde quickly recovered from his transition losses and moved through the rest of the front group alongside Shachar Sagiv (ISR).

The front two continued to push the pace and began adding time to Wilde behind. Hidalgo made his move before the second lap, and Hauser wasn’t able to respond. He quickly began to lose ground as the Brazilian looked comfortable all the way to the finish, taking the tape with an unmatched 14:20 5km.

According to recent reports, it was a much-needed WTCS win to carry momentum into the 2027 Triathlon World Tour. Hauser shared afterward that he “could really feel the legs – and the whole year – in the back end of that race.”.

Industry observers note that wilde crossed the line in third, comfortably ahead of the rest of the field, but a 14:52 5km left him short of the run speed he is accustomed to producing in these races. He won’t have much time to digest the result, however, as he immediately has to travel to Dubai, where he would look to continue his dominant T100 season.

Latest Update: How to Address Common Causes of Knee Pain While Cycling

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Fortunately, the culprit is often an easy fix, but the first step is to identify what may be causing your knee pain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as a cyclist, you probably know that you should always listen to your knees and the messages they send when they’re not so happy. These messages show up as aches and pains, and they’re common among those who ride. While research suggests cycling can actually help you avoid knee pain later in life, other studies indicate it still affects about 15 to 30 percent of cyclists.

Fortunately, the culprit is often an easy fix, but the first step is to identify what may be causing your knee pain. For example, you may be overtraining and pushing your body harder than it’s used to, straining your connective tissues and causing inflammation and pain.

Industry observers note that any spontaneous twinges of crank-stopping knee pain may feel like they come out of no where, when actually they’re just the first noticeable symptoms of a long-brewing problem. This generally stems from equipment and/or bike position problems, claims bike-fit specialist Michael Veal of BikeDynamics in Warwickshire, England.

“Many cyclists are forever tinkering with their position, looking for that elusive perfect position,” he indicates. But what feels just right for a few pedal strokes around the block can end up feeling pretty wrong after 70 miles of roads. A good bike fit is essential for preventing most causes of knee pain.

For more guidance on what your knee pain means and strategies to avoid it, read on.

In a recent development, WANT MORE INFO ON BIKE FIT? CHECK OUT OUR EXCLUSIVE PROGRAM!

To help you figure out where to start, here are the most common types of cycling knee pain and the ways in which your bike fit may contribute to each symptom.

If your knee hurts right on the cap (or patella), it’s typically because of your quads. The four quadricep muscles attach to the shin via the patella, and when you’re putting force into your pedal stroke, these muscles deliver that force across the knee joint.

Your bike set-up can help with this problem. Determine whether adjusting your saddle height, saddle fore and aft, and/or crank length could alleviate the problem. Working with a professional bike fitter can be extremely helpful in addressing this type of knee pain.

Industry observers note that “A saddle that is too low will keep your knee angle too tight at the top of the stroke, which increases the shear forces pulling the patella against the femur, which in turn increases the likelihood of tendonitis and harmful stresses in the cartilage behind the kneecap,” Veal says. “Likewise when the cranks are too long for your leg length, the knee joint is also too tight at the top of the stroke.”.

How low is too low for a saddle? “For a quick reference to check if your saddle is the right height, have a seat and rest your heel on the pedal with the pedal in the 6 o’clock position,” says fit specialist and physical therapist Sara Bresnick, founder of Pedal Power Training Solutions in Medford, Massachusetts. “The knee of that leg should be straight. That equates to a 20- to 25-degree knee bend when clipped in.”.

Riding with your saddle too far forward also can cause knee pain in the front, says Veal. “Your saddle should be positioned so the tibial tuberosity—or the bony bit below the kneecap—is directly above the ball of the foot, which in turn should be above the pedal spindle,” she says.

It has been revealed that also, be mindful of your form. Big-gear mashing, climbing in monster gears, and hard sprinting (especially if you’re not conditioned for it) can put undue stress on the knee and cause this type of pain.

If you do achieve a solid bike fit and avoid these common mistakes, and pain still persists, focus on stretching the quads to find relief.

Pain behind the knee is less common than pain in the front, and is generally easier to trace back to a culprit: over-extending the knee, indicates Bresnick. Your saddle is too high or too far back. “Try lowering the saddle a bit or moving it forward a bit in relation to the handlebars,” she says.

Industry observers note that this pain is also more common among cyclists who spend a lot of time on fixed-gear bikes; When you ride fixed, you use your hamstrings to decelerate your pedal stroke, which can put the biceps femoris tendon (a hamstring muscle that runs down the back of your leg toward the outside of your knee) under too much load and irritate it. Giving your legs a break with some freewheeling now and then can also help.

If pain sticks around after making bike adjustments, try stretching the hamstrings regularly and avoid frequent out-of-saddle riding.

In a recent development, when you feel pain on the inner (or medial sides) of your knees, look down at your feet: Cleat placement is often a culprit, claims Veal. Your cleat position affects your Q-factor, which dictates how far apart your feet are laterally when pedaling.

Ideally, the spacing should be that the loads from your knees to your pedals are traveling vertically without pushing the knee inward or outward, which stresses the ligaments on either side of your knee and can lead to pain.

Cleats positioned too close to the insides of your cycling shoes increase the distance between your feet, which can stress the inside collateral ligaments and cause pain in the inner (or medial) sides of your knees.

Too much float in your pedals also can cause medial knee pain. A little float—about 4.5 degrees—is all you need to be comfortable and keep your knees from getting stressed.

While a professional can help you adjust cleat positioning, you can also have someone take a slow-motion video you riding on a trainer, recording movement from the front of the bike. Look for asymmetry between your left and right side.

Recent findings suggest that if you still feel pain on the inside of your knee after aligning your cleats, especially if it is a burning pain at rest or sharp pain when you start to walk or step up or down, you may have a type of bursitis. This pain typically improves with a warmup and stretching of the hip flexors and adductors (inner thighs).

Pain on the outer (or lateral) sides of the knees is often caused by iliotibial (IT) band syndrome—a stabbing pain that happens when the IT band (a fibrous connective tissue band that runs from the hip along the thigh to the tibia) becomes stressed and inflamed.

IT band issues can appear to come out of nowhere, and hurt most when the knee is at 20- to 30-degrees of flexion, like when you approach the 6 o’clock position and start to come back up.

Recent findings suggest that “Misaligned cleats that cause the foot to be excessively toed in can cause this,” states Veal. So can cleats that are placed too far to the outsides of the shoes, causing too narrow of a stance on the bike.

It has been revealed that if you think the cleats on your bike are misaligned, take your bike in for an adjustment. (A slow-mo video of you riding from the front can also help you see if your cleat positioning is to blame!).

Sources indicate that of course, what you do on your bike will also go a long way to promoting or alleviating knee pain. Here are some tips to assure it’s the latter.

Recent findings suggest that just as with most sports, a little warmup to get blood flowing and muscles primed is a good idea—so don’t skip it! As a general rule, aim for at least 15 minutes of moderate spinning before you attack the local climb or go hard on the flats.

Look at video of the pros in action, and you’ll notice their rapid and fluid pedal strokes. Try this drill to improve your pedal stroke: The next time you are going up your favorite climb, use a gear at least two teeth lower (thus easier) than usual. This higher cadence is easier on your joints. Think about making round circles as you pedal, not ovals.

According to recent reports, your first ride back after any extended amount of time off shouldn’t be five hours long. Instead, start with a lower mileage and build slowly.

Your body likes consistency, so when you alter equipment, your knees often protest. Whether you get a latest bike, new shoes, new pedals, or change stem length, go easy at first to give yourself time to adapt.

Recent findings suggest that riding in 40-degree weather with red, chapped knees is a recipe for trouble. Pros routinely cover their legs in training when the temperature is below 60 degrees—that’s why knee warmers exist!

While each individual’s tolerance will differ, there’s certainly no harm in keeping muscles and joints warm. By using warmers, you can easily slip them off mid-ride if you start to warm up.

Take note of what gear works best in certain weather conditions, so you can repeat on future rides.

Industry observers note that if knee pain persists, consider getting a professional bike fit. And no, we’re not talking about when a salesperson sets your seat height at purchase.

A professional bike fit should be an in-depth experience with a professionally trained fitter that includes an interview process, off-bike flexibility testing, and on-bike measurements and adjustments. Yes, it’s an investment (usually at least $200), but it’s worth it to ride pain-free. It could end up being the best money you ever spent on your cycling habit.

In a recent development, if you’re still experiencing cycling knee pain after doing everything mentioned above, including a professional bike fit, it may be caused by muscle imbalances instead—like weak glutes, hips, or core. It’s best to consult with a sports medicine physician and/or physical therapist to find the right course of treatment for you.

Industry observers note that john Vasudevan, M.D. is an associate professor at the University of Pennsylvania. He is board-certified in Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation and Sports Medicine. He is a Team Physician for UPenn Athletics and  medical director of the Broad Street Run and Philadelphia Distance Run, and previously for the Rock 'n' Roll Half-Marathon and Tri-Rock Triathlon in Philadelphia. He is a director of the running and endurance Sports Medicine Program at Penn Medicine. He has been in practice at the University of Pennsylvania since 2012.
