📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

When I lace up for a day on the dirt, I know my trail running shoes are the only thing separating me from the rocks, roots, and miles of pure, unadulterated trail shenanigans. Trail runners, simply put, are just built different. We rack up mud and rocks with our mileage, and that means we expect more from our gear than road runners while simultaneously abusing the hell out of it. Thanks to my location on the East Coast, I get to run on a huge variety of trails, from packed singletrack to rocky technical trails, to muddy backwoods fire roads, to sandy marsh basins. Basically, I hit all the surfaces, so when I’m testing my trail shoes, I’m really digging in, and so is our legion of shoe testers.

According to recent reports, this year has been an interesting year for trail running shoes. Thanks to the growing popularity of trail running, there are more coming out than ever before, but because they are so specialized, reviews are generally all over the place. That’s why on this list you will see very specific workouts for every trail running shoe that we recommend. It’s also why I strategy on updating it pretty often, and hopefully expanding the list as new shoes come out and we get our wear testers running in them. The major brands we all expect to see on this list are on here: Saucony, Altra, Salomon, and the like, but choosing trail shoes is complicated and personal, so make sure you read through these reviews to determine which are the best trail running shoes for how and where you run.

Recent findings suggest that for over half a century, Runner’s World has been putting shoes through their paces with staff members and our diverse group of wear testers. These are everyday runners who hit the trailhead and make their shoes work. Every shoe I ran in was put through miles of testing based on its specificity—trail, gravel, technical shoes, et cetera. We evaluate for fit, grip, comfort, responsiveness, weather adaptability, and temperature regulation.

Recent findings suggest that the Hoka Speedgoat 7 makes you forget the problems of the 5 and 6. They’ve nailed the fit this time with updated uppers, new midsole foams, and a smarter construction that finally fixes those nagging complaints about the fit and feel. This model is seriously dialed-in now, making it the perfect shoe for flying over dusty, sandy trails where you need reliable grip without the gunk.

According to recent reports, stack height bumps to 36mm heel, 29mm forefoot using supercritical EVA foam for softer landings and snappier energy return, contrasting to the 6’s firmer feel. A winged heel counter and refined jacquard mesh upper with the addition of a gaiter mean these hug securely without hot spots or blisters, ditching the predecessor’s problems.

Sources indicate that vibram Megagrip outsole upgrades to 5mm lugs with deeper siping and wider spacing; they shed sandy dust and rail trail grit effortlessly while biting hardpack and mild roots. No rock plate keeps it light and easy.

Testers hail the 7’s plush stability on dusty rails—lugs channel sand away for consistent traction; upcoming foam eats vibration from chatter without mush. Uppers breathe during hot days and lock miles better than the 6 ever did.

Wear-tester Diane Grim did note they run a bit smaller, so sizing up is recommended for many, especially those hitting long distances, but she loved the improved fit over the 6, and notes that “the lug pattern placement was awesome in gripping (trails were snow-covered and snowmobile groomed),” and she “loved how the lugs continue under the toes for pushing off grip.”.

“The Speedgoat 7 engulfs your foot, giving you the security and confidence to get the job done,” she notes.

According to recent reports, the shoe is a great upgrade for singletrack/rail trail runners craving reliability on flowing, gritty paths from our breakdown. It’s less for pure rock slams, but dusty cruisers never felt this good.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

Recent findings suggest that salomon Pulsar Trail is a win for us for so many reasons, but the entry point of about $140 is hard to beat. It’s built for runners transitioning from roads or tackling milder trails, blending speed with everyday durability.

Sources indicate that this shoe rocks a 29mm heel stack and 23mm forefoot (6mm drop), delivering moderate cushion via TPU-based optiFoam². An Energy Blade TPU insert adds responsive pop and stability without bulk, making strides feel snappy yet protected.

The SensiFit upper with Quicklace locks your foot into the shoe—heel to toe—while breathable mesh keeps swamp feet at bay. The All Terrain Contagrip outsole features 4mm lugs for solid grip on dry dirt, gravel, and roots; it sheds mud decently but slips more on wet rocks.

No rock plate keeps weight low at 9.8 ounces, ideal for non-technical runs.

Wear-tester Rebecca Heflin praises the shoe’s comfort, stability, and versatility, wearing it from road to trail.

“The firmness of the sneaker keeps my foot more in place and safe,” she states. “They took a run or two to break in but then were much more flexible. You could ‘feel’ the ground and what you were running on, but still felt comfortable.” This has largely been my experience as well. For a shoe with some heft, it’s nimble and easy to run in.

The Pulsar Trail has a stable ride; it’s plush underfoot and has Salomon’s signature snug fit. Road-to-trail types will love the smooth pavement transitions. It’s perfect for gravel or mixed surfaces from our earlier breakdown.

Shop Men’s on salomon.com | Shop Women’s on Salomon.com.

Industry observers note that saucony Peregrine 16 delivers aggressive trail performance with major upgrades, and a less aggressive drop for a closer-to-the-ground feel. It’s our top pick for technical runners hitting rocks, roots, and mud, thanks to the fact that it’s now softer and grippier than ever.

Stack height hits 32mm heel and 28mm forefoot, powered by more Pwrrun foam for smoother cushioning on long hauls. A Pwrrun+ sockliner is made to add another layer of cushioning and, gross enough, smell issues. But I’ve noticed it also helps protect your feet from creepy crawlies and mud incursion. (Creepy crawlies being the most crucial by a mile.).

The upper has a snug heel and midfoot with a wider forefoot for toe splay, but not too much that it feels unstable or gives you “squishy toes.” They’re using durable, breathable mesh plus enhanced toe and underfoot protection. A Vibram Megagrip outsole with 4mm lugs grips hard on wet rocks, loose dirt, snow, and roots. The traction is significantly improved over prior models despite shallower depth.

It has been revealed that A rock guard plate shields from sharp jabs. And contrary to some other plated trail shoes, it doesn’t feel like you’re running on a cement brick. It’s light and protective without compromising foot motion.

In a recent development, wear-tester Diane Grim says of the Peregrine 16s, “I LOVE this shoe! Right out of the box, amazing! Lightweight, super comfortable, deep responsive vibram lugs.” She added that though the forefoot was stiff, the shoe eventually conformed to her foot after breaking it in. Lastly, she noted the rock plate and cushioning protected her feet from jabs as she ran over sharp rocks.

The Peregrine 16 fits technical trail types perfectly from our breakdown: deep lugs and armor for rocky descents. The shoe is versatile for mixed or singletrack, too.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

According to recent reports, I wasn’t sure if I’d like a trail shoe with Adidas’s energy rods. It didn’t feel like a natural pairing, but I’m sold. The impact protection and bit of easy sturdiness they add is genius. The Lightstrike Pro midsole makes the shoe feel fast, peppy, and fun even on unforgiving surfaces.

In a recent development, that’s the thing that keeps surprising me: I can run hard rock trail for hours and my feet just never come up. I train at ultra distances, and that can murder your feet. These just didn’t.

Some of our testers said the fit was narrow. If you’ve got a wide foot, try before you buy. The flip side is the upper mesh wraps really well once it breaks in, so you get that molded, locked-in feel without cranking the laces. Breathability is fine. Not stuffy, not airy either. On a hot day you’ll notice it.

Where I’d hesitate is technical scrambling: Anything steep and hands-on, anything where you’re placing a foot on an edge and trusting it, and the height and softness start working against you—it gets tippy.So: long runnable rocky stuff, absolutely. Chunky scrambles, I’d grab something lower and firmer.

Shop Men’s at adidas.com | Shop Women’s at adidas.com.

In a recent development, altra Experience Wild 3 is a fave for road-to-trail trekkers, making mixed surfaces like macadam, packed gravel, and light dirt paths seem easy. Its low-drop design and wide toebox allow for natural strides on urban-trail mashups without the clunk of pure trail beasts.

Sources indicate that stack height clocks 32mm with cushioned but snappy Ego P35 foam for responsive cushion that feels efficient, not mushy. An extremely subtle rocker aids smooth transitions from asphalt to gravel chatter.

According to recent reports, the engineered mesh upper fits securely yet roomy up front, with durable overlays and gaiter traps to block debris on chip seal or cracked pavement trails. MaxTrac outsole packs 4mm lugs that grip macadam’s rough texture, dry gravel, and hardpack without slipping, shedding light mud pretty decently. No rock plate keeps it nimble, prioritizing speed over heavy armor.

Sources indicate that wear-tester John Mikovits raves about the Experience Wild 3, saying, “I loved the way the shoe slipped onto my foot and laced up. The upper felt plenty roomy like many within the brand but also felt secure in the midfoot and heel.

“The midfoot felt secure which kept me in place when pivoting, turning, and both up/downhills,” he added. “I felt secure for the whole ride and really did not notice any feeling of lack of stability or [the shoe being] too loose.”.

Daily training, tempo efforts, or 10 to 20 mile mixed runs thrive here; it’s forgiving for road runners dipping into trails. Though less ideal for steep tech or deep slop, it crushes with efficiency and comfort on crumbly-heavy routes that blend pavement and dirt.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

Recent findings suggest that lululemon Wildfeel is a truly versatile trail shoe that’s made for runners who live on flowing singletrack and smooth rail trails. It combines plush comfort and reliable grip for those easy, sometimes muddy, sometimes sandy miles where the path can be unpredictable, and staying nimble is key.

Recent findings suggest that the midsole has dual-density supercritical foam with a cushier heel for shock absorption, and a firmer forefoot for responsive toe-off. This setup helps with stability on undulating singletrack and groomed rail trails.

It has been revealed that the sock-like Nulu-lined upper with Lycra-nylon hugs your ankle, acting sort of as a gaiter to block debris on dusty, buggy singletrack. The high-abrasion outsole has 4mm multi-directional lugs that bite reliably on dry dirt, roots, and hardpack rail paths, handling light mud and uneven sections without making you feel wibbly-wobbly.

According to recent reports, tester Ryan Werling loves the Wildfeel, saying, “I looked forward to my runs in this shoe and I felt very confident on any surface (declines/inclines). I have tested some very good trail shoes in this program but the Wildfeel is number one so far.” He did note a less-breathable upper, but here’s the thing: that sealed upper makes it perfect for handling super gross surfaces and sandy marsh trails.

In a recent development, the Wildfeel is less suited for super-technical steeps or deep slop. However, it nails versatile, fun performance on singletrack/rail trail.

Shop Men’s at lululemon.com | Shop Women’s at lululemon.com.

Recent findings suggest that nike’s ACG (All Conditions Gear) line has leveled up lately, and the Zegama Trail is where I’m the most impressed. When the ground turns to oatmeal and the grass is banana-peel slippery, this is the shoe I reach for. The Vibram outsole and aggressive, opposed checkmark lugs dig into packed dirt, wet rock, and sloppy singletrack without ever clogging up. They stay clean and grippy so you can point your nose downhill and trust it.

The revised last is the real upgrade over the old model: it cups the outer rim of your foot so completely that it almost reads as a stability shoe underfoot. A stitched finger loop at the heel makes them easy to yank on, and they breathe well without feeling drafty. My one nitpick is a split in the lug pattern near the heel you can feel on steep descents. They’re a touch heavier than past versions, but I never noticed once moving. As tester Chris Fisher put it, “a solid comfortable trail shoe that I have enjoyed.”.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

The Mount To Coast H1 absolutely shreds as a gravel specialist, engineered for lightning-fast fire roads and packed paths where loose stones and chatter try to throw you off your game. Its 6mm drop and minimalist build turn rugged gravel into a smooth, efficient run zone that’s ditching the bulk of tech-trail shoes.

Stack height measures 28mm heel, 22mm forefoot, and has a firm, responsive CircleCell foam midsole that delivers sharp ground feel and peppy energy return on washboard gravel. And a wide toebox is a big bonus for folks who love brands like Altra and Topo.

The featherweight mesh upper with minimal overlays breathes easy and fends off dust kicks. Custom sticky rubber outsole rocks 2mm-shallow, tightly patterned lugs that bite small gravel relentlessly while spacing sheds rocks and dirt fast—no clogging on dry, fast-packed surfaces.

The shoe weighs a scant 7.5 ounces for endless miles.

Testers love its razor-sharp handling on gravel—lugs lock in loose stones for zero slip, moderate drop eases calf strain on long efforts, low stack eats vibrations from rutted fire roads, and wide base shrugs off camber without wobble.

In a recent development, “The fit and comfort of the Mount To Coast is superb,” states tester Liz Fones. “The length felt true-to-size, and the width was generally well-balanced, offering plenty of room without feeling sloppy.”.

The H1 is a quintessential gravel shoe: light, grippy, and built for speed on packed dirt and crunchy paths.

Shop Men’s at mounttocoast.com | Shop Women’s at mounttocoast.com.

I am one of those sick, sick puppies who thinks that strapping on a pack and running 100 miles through the woods is a good time, and the On Cloudultra Pros are my upcoming favorite shoe to do that in. The On Cloudultra Pro dominates trail ultramarathons, built for 50K to 100-mile suffer-fests where relentless cushioning and durability outlast crumbling legs on technical singletrack and endless climbs.

Its beastly but comfy upper and upgraded foams turn multiday epics into (slightly) less painful slogs. Unfortunately, you do pay for the privilege as this is by far the priciest shoe on the list.

Stack height soars to 39mm heel, 35mm forefoot (4mm drop) powered by CloudTec Phase midsole pods—hollow chambers that compress for plush landings then rebound explosively for forward drive—paired with Helion HF Hyperfoam that stays springy across 200+ miles of abuse without packing out.

Sources indicate that the Swiss-engineered upper fuses a thermo-mapped, one-piece Speedboard chassis for rigidity and energy return, with reinforced Speed-Lacing and gaiter integration blocking debris on rooty, dusty ultras. Missiongrip outsole deploys 2.5mm lugs with cleat-like clusters that grip wet slabs, mud, and talus, while self-cleaning aggressively. The shoe is tank-like yet responsive.

I am crushing my 100-miler training, and I will be praising nonstop the joy of CloudTec comfort. I have no hot spots after my eight-hour run last week, thanks to the HF Hyperfoam’s fatigue-free bounce on rocky tech. I was stable through the most miles I’ve run this calendar year, and the foundation feels protective for heavy runners hauling packs. It’s built for comfort and brutality, and I plan on maxing both out.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com.

The Norda 055 is what happens when someone asks, “What if a hyper-technical trail shoe had a really good stack?” It’s an actual max-cushion mountain shoe with a 36mm stack in the heel and 30mm stack in the forefoot, so your quads get a soft landing while the rest of you commits to the descent.

The preferred shoe of ultrarunner Rachel Entrekin, the upper is woven from bio-circular Dyneema, a fiber with a strength-to-weight ratio 15 times that of steel. You can’t kill these shoes, and I know this because I’ve done my best to try. The knit sock collar keeps trail grit outside your shoe, so the only thing getting into your socks is the gross sweat of your feet.

This is a shoe that gets better with miles, which is rare. Not that it needs breaking in, but there’s a magic in the way the shoe relaxes. The 055 is a sturdy and nimble training partner on the mountain, easily handling wicked terrain, water, mud, and at least one German shepherd.

Industry observers note that yes, it costs $325. But it’s the long-haul, ultra-distance, “I have a spreadsheet for my aid stations” shoe. Per mile, it’s a bargain, and you can quote me on that when you explain it to whoever manages your budget.

It has been revealed that it’s stable, explosive, and rugged. Basically the Linux kernel of footwear, but it actually looks good. (P.S. I only know what that is because my kid just explained that whole thing to me last night.).

Shop Men’s at nordarun.com | Shop Women’s at nordarun.com.

Trail shoes consist of four main parts: uppers, midsoles, outsoles, and rock plates. These components work together for protection, cushioning, traction, and durability on everything from gravel to gnarly singletrack.

In a recent development, uppers form the breathable shell around your foot. They feature tough mesh with rubber overlays at the toes and heels to fend off rocks, roots, and trail debris while staying ventilated.

Midsoles provide the cushioning core, typically using EVA foam or advanced compounds like TPU or supercritical foams. They absorb shock from uneven ground and return energy to keep your legs fresh over long miles.

Sources indicate that outsoles are the grippy foundation with lugs made from sticky rubber compounds such as Vibram Megagrip. Lug depth and pattern vary by terrain: multidirectional for mud, clustered for rocks, all designed to shed debris and last through abrasion.

Recent findings suggest that rock plates sit between midsole and outsole as thin shields of plastic, aluminum, or carbon fiber. They protect against sharp stones and roots without adding much weight or stifling flexibility. With max cushioned trail shoes, they’re not necessarily a must-have anymore, though many runners still prefer them. They don’t exist in every trail shoe, and in the case where a trail shoe may have a carbon plate, it can add protection and stability.

Trail shoes specialize by terrain to optimize weight, grip, and protection. Choosing the right type means less slip, less fatigue, and more fun no matter the surface.

According to recent reports, drop refers to the heel-to-toe height difference, ranging from 0mm (zero drop for natural foot positioning) to 15mm (higher for calf relief on roads or long efforts). Low drops (0 to 4mm) build foot strength but demand adaptation; 8 to 12mm suits most runners.

Stack height measures total midsole thickness underfoot, outsole, and footbed—usually 20 to 35mm at the heel and slightly less at the forefoot. Max stack (30mm+) offers plush protection for heavy runners or rocky miles; low stack (under 25mm) delivers precise ground feel for agile, technical runs.

According to recent reports, gore-Tex and similar membranes laminate into uppers to block liquid water and wind while venting sweat vapor for a little bit of breathability. They shine in rain, snow, or mud, often paired with mesh drainage ports and quick-lace systems to handle stream crossings without sogginess.

I’ve scrubbed enough mud from lugs to write a whole damn article on it, because nothing tanks your trail high like dried clumps firing off mid-stride. Hit them with the hose right after runs to loosen crud and clean them off. Use an old natural bristle brush and mild soap to excavate lug crevices, then stuff with newspaper or paper towels to speed drying. Never toss in the washer; it wrecks glue and mesh. Insider hack: let the muddiest shoes that you can’t get to right away dry out and then bang off the mud. It works, I promise.

For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. It has been revealed that the S&P 500 is an index that tracks the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the United States, weighted by market capitalization. It includes Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Berkshire Hathaway, and approximately 493 other companies that collectively represent about 80% of the total U.S. stock market value.

The index is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, which periodically adds and removes companies based on criteria including market cap (must exceed ~$18 billion), profitability, liquidity, and domicile. When a tech giant is added to the S&P 500, every index fund tracking it automatically buys shares — and vice versa when companies are removed.

According to recent reports, an S&P 500 index fund is a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds all 500 stocks in the same proportions as the index. Instead of picking individual stocks, you buy one fund and instantly own a piece of every major U.S. company. The fund mechanically replicates the index — no stock picking, no market timing, no overpaid fund managers.

The data is overwhelming. Over any 15-year period, approximately 92% of actively managed large-cap funds underperform the S&P 500 after fees, according to the SPIVA scorecard. Over 20 years, that number exceeds 95%. The reasons are simple: active fund managers charge 0.50% to 1.50% in annual fees, they generate taxable trading activity, and they cannot consistently pick winners.

Recent findings suggest that warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. He won decisively — the index fund returned 125.8% vs 36.0% for the hedge fund basket. As Buffett has said: "By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals.".

Recent findings suggest that the top S&P 500 index funds deliver nearly identical performance because they all track the same index. The differences come down to expense ratio, minimum investment, fund structure (ETF vs mutual fund), and tax efficiency. Here is a detailed comparison of the five most popular options.

Sources indicate that the most popular S&P 500 ETF and the default recommendation for most FI seekers. At 0.03% expense ratio, a $500,000 investment costs just $150 per year in fees. VOO is tax-efficient due to the ETF structure and Vanguard's patented heartbeat trade process, which minimizes capital gains distributions. Fractional shares are available at most brokerages.

In a recent development, the lowest-cost S&P 500 fund available at 0.015% — half the cost of VOO. No minimum investment requirement makes it ideal for beginners. As a mutual fund, you can set up automatic investments in exact dollar amounts (e.g., $500/month). FXAIX is an excellent choice if your brokerage is Fidelity.

Sources indicate that blackRock's S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio, matching VOO. Functionally identical performance. Slightly different creation/redemption mechanics than VOO but the practical difference for individual investors is negligible. A strong alternative if you prefer iShares or trade through a brokerage that offers commission-free iShares ETFs.

The oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 ETF, rolled out in 1993. SPY is the most liquid ETF in the world, making it the preferred choice for active traders. However, its 0.0945% expense ratio is over three times higher than VOO or IVV. For long-term FI investors, VOO or IVV are better choices. SPY's structure as a unit investment trust also makes it slightly less tax-efficient than VOO.

Schwab's mutual fund offering at 0.02% expense ratio with no minimum investment. Like FXAIX, the mutual fund structure allows automatic dollar-amount investing. An excellent choice for Schwab customers building automated investment plans.

For retirement accounts (401k, IRA), look for the S&P 500 index fund option within your strategy. It may have a different name (e.g., "Large Cap Index Fund" or "Institutional S&P 500") but will track the same index.

It has been revealed that the total stock market index (tracked by VTI/VTSAX/FSKAX) holds approximately 3,600 stocks compared to the S&P 500's 500. The additional 3,100 stocks are mid-cap and small-cap companies. Here is how they compare:.

Historically, the performance difference between the two is minimal — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year in either direction. The S&P 500 has outperformed in periods when large-cap growth stocks dominate. The total market has outperformed when small and mid-cap stocks lead. Over 20+ year periods, the returns converge closely.

The FI community's honest answer: it does not matter much which you choose. Investing $25,500 per year in VOO or VTI will produce nearly identical outcomes over 20 years. Consistency and contribution amount matter far more than the choice between S&P 500 and total market.

S&P 500 index funds typically yield 1.2% to 1.6% in annual dividends. In a tax-advantaged account (401k, IRA, Roth), dividends compound tax-free. In a taxable account, qualified dividends from S&P 500 funds are taxed at the favorable long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

Industry observers note that ETFs (VOO, IVV) are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) in taxable accounts because ETFs rarely distribute capital gains. Vanguard's mutual funds are an exception — their patented ETF share class structure gives Vanguard mutual funds ETF-like tax efficiency. For taxable brokerage accounts, VOO or VFIAX (Vanguard's mutual fund version) are the most tax-efficient choices.

The most common mistake with S&P 500 index funds is waiting for the "right time" to invest. Research from Vanguard highlights that investing a lump sum immediately outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets go up more often than they go down. Missing just the 10 best trading days over a 20-year period can cut your returns nearly in half. If you have money to invest, the data overwhelmingly says to invest it now — not next week, not after the next pullback, not when it "feels right.".

In a recent development, open an account at Vanguard (for VOO/VFIAX), Fidelity (for FXAIX), or Schwab (for SWPPX). All three offer commission-free trading on their own index funds, excellent customer service, and robust retirement account options. You can also buy any of these funds at most brokerages.

ETFs (VOO, IVV) trade like stocks at real-time prices and are more tax-efficient in taxable accounts. Mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) allow automatic dollar-amount investing and are better for set-it-and-forget-it contribution schedules. For retirement accounts, either works equally well.

Transfer cash to your brokerage account and buy your chosen fund. Start with whatever you have — there is no minimum too small. FXAIX and SWPPX have $0 minimums, and VOO can be purchased in fractional shares at most brokerages for as little as $1.

According to recent reports, automate monthly or per-paycheck contributions. This removes emotion from the process and ensures consistent dollar-cost averaging. Most brokerages let you schedule recurring purchases of mutual funds. For ETFs, some brokerages offer automatic ETF purchases as well.

If you hold other asset classes (bonds, international), rebalance once per year to maintain your target allocation. Otherwise, do nothing — do not check daily prices, do not sell during downturns, and do not chase performance. The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in history. Time in the market beats timing the market.

Fidelity 500 Index Fund (FXAIX) has the lowest expense ratio at 0.015%. Schwab S&P 500 Index Fund (SWPPX) is next at 0.02%. VOO and IVV tie at 0.03%. All four are excellent — the fee difference between FXAIX (0.015%) and VOO (0.03%) on a $500,000 portfolio is just $75 per year. Choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage.

VOO is better for long-term investors. It charges 0.03% vs SPY's 0.0945%, saving you about $325 per year on a $500,000 portfolio. VOO is also more tax-efficient due to its ETF share class structure. SPY's advantage is liquidity for active trading, which long-term index investors do not need. For buy-and-hold FI investing, VOO is the clear winner.

In a recent development, either is an excellent choice. The S&P 500 covers approximately 80% of the U.S. stock market by value. A total market fund adds mid-cap and small-cap stocks for fuller diversification. Over long periods, performance is nearly identical — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year. The FI community consensus is that the best fund is the one you will consistently invest in without overthinking the decision.

Industry observers note that as little as $1. FXAIX and SWPPX have zero minimum investments. VOO and IVV can be purchased as fractional shares at most brokerages. There is no minimum too small — starting with $50 or $100 per month and increasing contributions as your income grows is exactly how most people on the FI path begin.

Industry observers note that the S&P 500 has returned approximately 10.3% per year on average since 1957 (including dividends). Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7.0% per year. These are long-term averages — individual years range from -38% (2008) to +38% (1995). The key is staying invested through the down years to capture the recovery gains that follow.

In a recent development, S&P 500 index funds carry market risk — they can lose significant value in the short term (the index dropped 34% in early 2020 and 38% in 2008). However, the S&P 500 has recovered from every decline in its history and has never lost money over any 20-year period. For investors with a 10+ year time horizon, the risk of not investing (missing out on 10% average annual returns) is far greater than the risk of temporary market declines.

S&P 500 index funds are the single most crucial building block for long-term wealth. With expense ratios as low as 0.015%, you keep virtually all of your returns while owning a piece of the 500 largest U.S. companies. VOO, FXAIX, IVV, and SWPPX all deliver near-identical performance — choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage and automate your contributions. The FI community has proven through thousands of real-world examples that consistent investing in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, held for decades without panic selling, is the most reliable path to building wealth and reaching financial independence.

Recent findings suggest that brooks wanted to change what we should expect when running in a max-cushioned trainer. “We noticed that for some people, they would start running in a neutral shoe and then their body would work extra. So the internal cost was actually increasing,” said Brooks Footwear PLM and BlueLine Director Nikhil Jain.

Sources indicate that the team set out to create a shoe that would cut that internal cost. The Glycerin Flex has a decoupled heel and Flex Zone; these components allow your foot to flex naturally instead of working against a stiff, beefy platform.

“Testing the Brooks Glycerin Flex was a novel experience for me on multiple fronts,” said Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Not only was this the first Brooks running shoe I’ve ever run in, but it was also the first hyperflexible shoe that I have ever seen—and overall, it was a positive experience. The Glycerin Flex combines the benefits of a daily trainer that allows your feet to work and get stronger with the comfort and protection of a maximalist shoe.”.

We like the Glycerin Max 2 for run/walking and recovery days. The shoe has 45 mm of DNA Tuned foam in the heel and a 6 mm offset. Its beefiness was off-putting for some, especially for runners hoping to get in some tempo work on their long runs. But testers remarked the cushioning was extremely comfy on slow days.

Sources indicate that “I loved how comfortable the sneaker was. I instantly felt supported and it felt like I was walking on a bouncy pillow,” said wear-tester Steph Norman. “This sneaker would be great for easy/long miles where you do not have to worry about your feet hurting.”.

It has been revealed that the popular Brooks Ghost hits the trails. The shoe is outfitted for going off-road with 3 mm lugs on the TrailTack rubber outsole.

Our tester, David Hinkl, appreciated how the shoe protected his feet on gnarly surfaces. “The best part of the shoe for me was the sole,” he said. “It was beefy enough to prevent sharp rocks and pointy things from getting to my feet. The Canopy is iconic. Despite the curtains of rain, monstrous winds, and cold temps, Des Linden was the first American woman to win the 2018 Boston Marathon after 33 years. Industry observers note that the Run Visible not only ensures you’re seen with reflective detail, but it also keeps you warm thanks to Thermolite insulation. Three pockets provide storage. That hi-vis orange color also helps you pop out in low light.

Our Editors Ride-Tested Virginia Tech’s Top-Rated Road and Gravel Helmets—Including a $60 Pick That Punches Way Above Its Price

  • As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times.
  • When shopping for fresh road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a new helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

When shopping for fresh road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

Recent findings suggest that so, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? Presently, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

It has been revealed that virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

Sources indicate that “The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” says Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

Virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a upcoming helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

In a recent development, editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

According to recent reports, “Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

All of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

The Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

According to recent reports, for a newly introduced brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the company grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

Sources indicate that the POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically significant lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

It has been revealed that the Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

In our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina said it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

Sources indicate that P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

Sources indicate that the one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on said it was a little snug near their temples.

Given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Recent findings suggest that unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

Ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

Of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

The Triathlete editorial team has been around long enough that we’ve collectively written dozens of holiday gift guides — from stocking stuffers to price point round-ups to personality-based ideas, always solid ideas but usually pretty generic.

Sources indicate that but this year, we wanted to get more personal and spread some holiday cheer along the way. So the editors made a list of some of our most consistent writers and hand-selected gifts to match each of them. We sent the gifts to their doors and hoped we’d hit the mark.

And we are happy to share our IRL gift ideas with you for your own gifting or wish list creation. Below, you’ll find out a little bit more about some of our favorite contributors, what we gifted them, and why we think they’ll enjoy it.

About the contributor: Sara is lucky enough to live in the triathlete’s dream training locale: Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, home of the Ironman World Championship. Though there’s lots to envy, I’m particularly green over her access to daily open-water swimming. But I also worry because swimming in open water comes with more risks than the typical pool.

Industry observers note that what we gifted (and why): Sara’s frequent open-water swimming is why I’m gifting her this safety buoy from Tri-Fit. It’s bright, so she’s visible to other swimmers and from shore, and stable in the water if she needs to use it to adjust her goggles or shake off a calf cramp. But wait, there’s more! What I really love about this buoy is that it goes beyond your standard safety product – it’s an actual training workhorse, with a 1-liter hydration bladder and bite valve for days when Sara decides she wants to swim with the dolphins and sea turtles a little longer.

In a recent development, about the contributor: Sierra is a skilled writer who has lent her talents to highlight the need for more athlete-friendly pregnancy and postpartum deferral policies and to advocate for clearer policies around breastfeeding and pumping during races. She’s a mom to an active toddler.

What we gifted (and why): Life as a mom is busy and includes plenty of extras – like the armful of toys your child just has to bring with them to leave the house. As a fellow mom, I know what it feels like to not have enough arms to hold all the water bottles, snacks, and gear that comes with both triathlon and motherhood, so a bag with a pocket for everything can be a ready-made way of getting out of the house for training in an organized state, even when life as a mom feels far from organized.

—Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

In a recent development, about the contributor: Emma-Kate is a retired professional triathlete who’s still very much involved in the sport while continuing to multisport train and lift regularly. From her home in Boulder, Colorado, she interviews experts, talks to today’s top pro athletes, and writes to make changes and news of the sport understandable to all athletes.

Recent findings suggest that what we gifted (and why): Winters in Colorado are long and cold, making training challenging. As a tri nerd, I think Emma-Kate will enjoy keeping up with her training indoors using the latest swim tech. While I don’t think ZWIM will keep her from the gym (I’m not sure anything could), I do think it will complement her training nicely to make the winter not feel so long.

Industry observers note that about the contributor: Tim is one of my favorite storytellers in triathlon, and I feel lucky to not only get to edit his stories regularly, but to hear the stories behind the stories. I can’t repeat most of them in print, but trust me when I say Tim Heming has seen some wild stuff.

Industry observers note that what we gifted (and why): Naturally, when I read Mike Reilly’s book, Finding Your Finish Line, I thought of Tim. Reilly, also known as the “Voice of Ironman,” announced over 350,000 athletes across the finish line during his career as a race announcer before retiring in 2022. He, too, has seen it all, and some of his best tales are in this book. If I could get Tim and Mike in the same room to swap stories, it would probably be the best day of my triathlon career.

Reilly’s book, co-written with Triathlete contributor Sarah Wassner Flynn, is a masterful piece of storytelling. It’s inspirational, aspirational, and will leave you feeling proud to be a triathlete.

According to recent reports, about the contributor: Susan is a board-certified sports dietitian, accomplished Ironman athlete and Kona qualifier, and runs her own business helping endurance athletes dial in their health and performance goals through their nutrition. She is our go-to writer whenever we need a sports nutrition concept or topic broken down in a way that triathletes can apply to their own training and racing.

It has been revealed that what we gifted (and why): I’ve been a long-time fan of Skratch Labs for its simple ingredients and clean flavors. When we saw Skratch now offers a make-it-yourself gel-making kit using its super high-carb sports drink mix, we thought the nutrition expert who literally wrote our guide on high-carb fueling might enjoy easily customizing her nutrition intake. More than the fueling customization, the kit also provides a less gooey gel texture and planet-friendly reusable soft flasks. I’m eager to hear how it works for her!

—Bethany Mavis, contributing editor.

About the contributor: When college student Saqib came on board as an intern in our Endurance department, the first question I had for this gangly cross-country runner was, “Have you done a triathlon?” The answer was no, and I am making it my life’s mission to change that.

What we gifted (and why): Did Saqib ask for resources on triathlon? He did not. In fact, he thinks of himself as a land animal and has no interest in swimming, which is why I’m gifting him this book from Triathlete contributor Alison Freeman – just to plant the seed. Isn’t that what holiday gifts are for, anyway? Subtle hints wrapped in shiny paper? I think of my brother-in-law, who always gifts his wife exercise equipment even though she is a couch potato; or my mother, who has given me countless hairstyling tools to tame my wild mane into something she deems more respectable.

But this book will actually serve its purpose, because Freeman has a real talent for making a significant, scary goal like a first triathlon approachable and achievable. Her book is a start-to-finish roadmap that eliminates guesswork and leaves the reader feeling like they can not only do a triathlon, but also have fun along the way.

About the contributor: Jon Dorn is a former editor, longtime triathlete, and lifetime gear geek. He’s qualified for six age-group world championships, and loves to bust his butt training for long-course tri. If I hear about a cutting-edge piece of gear, an unconventional training method, or something that’s just plain weird, I call Jon. That stated, he’s not afraid to call a spade a spade and let me know if something is just pricey junk; he’s no fanboy.

What we gifted (and why): I had heard about red light therapy in the context of the general health/beauty space for a few years, but it wasn’t until I was wandering the expo in Kona at this year’s Ironman World Championship that I encountered a red light therapy device that not only targeted triathletes but is also portable. Sadly, the one I checked out on the Major Island was bonkers expensive and didn’t make sense for a gift, so I shopped around for something similar that wouldn’t break the bank. I landed on the reasonably priced Valo Spark that had decent reviews.

In a recent development, on one hand, I’m not 100% sold on the efficacy of red light therapy — and the science is still out on how it works with sports-related aches and pains — but I know Jon trains super hard (his next race is Boulder 70.3 in June), I know he has his share of aches and pains, I know he loves to travel, and I know he likes trying new things. Whether he loves it or uses it as a portable night light, I can’t wait to find out what he thinks!

The SP Force AXS is our flagship triathlon bike, with a full carbon fiber frame and bars, built with SRAM Force electronic shifting and Zipp 404 Firecrest Carbon wheels. If you want the best performance along with the best value in triathlon, now’s your chance. Our limited BFCM sale is live now.

About the contributor: Arguably one of the most accomplished triathletes in Triathlete’s contributor lineup, with hundreds of triathlons and well over a dozen Ironmans under her belt, Jordan knows the sport from every perspective. She’s also one of the industry’s best-known and loved figures, representing professional athletes and helping brands grow their businesses.

It has been revealed that few people know the triathlon world better than Jordan, past or present. (She’s our first pick for a triathlon trivia team.) With her finger on the pulse, she gives pros and age-groupers a voice and digs into the stories shaping the sport.

What we gifted (and why): Jordan might spend more time in the saddle than any of us editors, and she knows her gear as well as anyone, especially what the pros are presently using. While she’s at the moment on the road to recovery from a meniscus tear, we wanted to send her something custom and pro-level to test whether the 3D investment matches the marketing as she rebuilds her fitness on the bike.

But saddles are tricky to gift. Finding this fully adjustable, 3D-printed option gave us the versatility we were looking for: a fit she could fine-tune herself, without being limited to the stock setup straight out of the box.

—Travis Mundell, social media manager.

Recent findings suggest that about the contributor: Zach Nehr is another one of our key tech/gear editors, especially when it comes to indoor training. Blessed (or cursed) by living in the not-winter-compatible state of Wisconsin, Zach is a die-hard Zwifty and has used probably just about every indoor trainer or virtual training platform that exists (or has existed). As much as Zach rides inside, I trust that if he says something is great, it’s great; if it’s not, it’s probably in the dumpster. Because you don’t ride inside as much as he does with junk.

Industry observers note that what we gifted (and why): The Profile Design Zwift Ride Supersonic Aerobar was a medium-quiet release during this year’s Hawaii Ironman World Championship week – mostly because you don’t think much about riding in the pain cave when you’re in a tropical paradise prepping for the biggest race of your season. As incongruous as the setting was for an indoor release, I was excited to see that Profile was taking its triathletes seriously by announcing the first-ever triathlon-specific Zwift-integrated aerobar for indoor training.

I wanted to gift this to Zach because if you dedicate enough time to training indoors, you should really dedicate your indoor training setup as well, not just make do. Being able to control your avatar from a dedicated set of Zwift Ride–compatible aerobars is the pinnacle of tri gear, as it completes the perfect pain cave: the kind that could prep you for next year’s Ironman World Championship, anyway.

Sources indicate that about the contributor: When it comes to explaining sports psychology and neuroscience studies to triathletes, there’s no one better than Daya. As a neuroscientist, certified mental performance consultant, and yogi, Daya helps all types of athletes train their brains through her business, and she can make even the nerdiest psychology studies understandable and applicable for triathletes.

What we gifted (and why): When we heard about the Muse Athena S Headband, a “brain-sensing headband,” we thought of Daya. The headband claims it can do everything from tracking your brainwave activity for better focus to tracking your blood oxygenation in the prefrontal cortex to help you build mental endurance. If anyone can sort through the science behind the Muse, it’s Daya, so we’re excited to hear how effective it seems to be in her own athletic performance.

#91316. Latest Update: Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1299 w)

Latest Update: Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree.
  • If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month.
  • In a recent development, but what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

In a recent development, but what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

According to recent reports, I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Sources indicate that before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the issue in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

So what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

According to recent reports, A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

Industry observers note that it’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

In a recent development, on one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

According to recent reports, the difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Recent findings suggest that those short efforts make the problem easy to see, but the difference showed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

On a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

It has been revealed that I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar challenges early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the matter. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The firm has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

If you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

Industry observers note that the significant problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

The easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

And yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

According to recent reports, test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most runners are familiar with the substantial muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes.
  • A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World.
  • When you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, states Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most runners are familiar with the substantial muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. But there are lesser-known—yet still important—players that can influence running performance. One example: the quadratus lumborum, or QL for short.

A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. It serves a few different functions in daily life, such as helping you arch your back, bend to the side, and rotate your upper body, Haas explains.

When you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, states Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group. The QL also assists with breathing, specifically when you inhale, Agnew adds.

In a recent development, if this muscle is tight or irritated, you’ll likely feel pain in your back or sacroiliac joints, which link the pelvis and lower spine, Agnew says. To help you avoid these aches, we asked the PTs to explain what can cause an angry QL and how to relieve it.

There are several reasons your QL might be yelling at you. A common one? Your hip flexors are tight. In particular, when the psoas (a significant, rope-like hip flexor muscle that runs from your lower back to the front of your hip) is shortened, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, meaning your pelvis is tipped forward, arching your lower back. In many cases, this yanks on your QL as well, because the psoas and QL both insert into the same group of vertebrae in your lower back, Agnew explains.

Another culprit is weak glutes. When your glutes aren’t strong enough to help you maintain good running mechanics, your knee can collapse inward as you land and your opposite-side hip can dip down, Haas explains. This, in turn, can cause your trunk to side bend and rotate, thus placing more strain on your QL over time. Running downhill can exacerbate the problem, Haas adds, because that can cause your lower back to arch and place further stress on your QL.

Recent findings suggest that yet another cause of an irritated QL is upper-back stiffness. Restrictions in the upper part of the spine can shift more workload onto the QL, Haas explains. So can issues in your shoulders, hips, and mid-back. If these areas aren’t moving like they should due to pain or injury, your QL may receive added stress, Haas says.

Keep in mind that in some cases, your QL may hurt because it’s taking on a bunch of extra stress it’s not meant to, but the muscle itself probably isn’t tight. “It’s more like your QL is just irritated because everything has been collapsing around it and loading it,” Haas claims. “It’s overworked and underappreciated.”.

According to recent reports, A tight-feeling QL is worth addressing because it can lead to a few not-so-great complications if left unchecked. A big one? Compromised running mechanics.

A tight QL, as mentioned, can shorten your hip flexors and pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, which will reduce your knee lift as you stride, Agnew says. As a result, “you’re not going to be able to generate as much force moving forward, and you’ll have more of an arched-back position when you run,” he explains. In many cases, this can deliver a double whammy of reduced performance and increased back pain, he says.

In a recent development, on top of that, a tight QL can also hinder your breathing. As mentioned above, one of the QL’s jobs is to help you inhale, so when this muscle is tight, you may not be able to breathe as deeply or easily, Agnew notes.

Plagued by what you think may be an irritated QL? Try Agnew’s three-step at-home series to help reduce your discomfort.

Perform this sequence as often as every day if you’re in significant discomfort that’s limiting your ability to run. In the case of minor pain, incorporate this series two to three times per week. On the days you run, perform the myofascial release, pelvic tilts, and hip hikes before you lace up, then tackle the other components afterward.

This can help turn down the pain response in a barking QL by desensitizing soft tissue, Agnew explains.

How to Perform Myofascial Release.

Industry observers note that the pelvic tilts help you learn how to coordinate and control pelvic motion so you can maintain proper mechanics while running, and the hip hikes help activate your QL. The kettlebell side bend increases blood flow to the muscle, which can aid in healing. Finally, the suitcase carry increases strength, stability, and engagement of the muscle, which can ensure it functions properly during a run.

Lengthen your QL—as well as tight hip flexors—with this two-for-one half-kneeling lunge stretch.

Do these moves daily or several times per day to mobilize your lower back. Perform them before or after a run. Vital caveat: If your QL hurts more after stretching—or if your QL pain returns soon after stretching—then stretches are likely not the solution and you should stop doing them, Haas explains.

Dynamic QL Mobility + Hip 90/90.

To start, do one set of these moves daily to help your body learn the neuromuscular patterns. (The caveat: If you feel sore, then skip a day.) After about six weeks, do these moves two to three times per week as part of your regular strength-training routine.

This exercise targets the glutes and works on pelvic control in a movement pattern that’s similar to running. Think of it as an opportunity to train proper glute use in your running form, which will help unload any strain on your QL caused by weak glutes.

Recent findings suggest that this exercise can improve core stability and strengthen the glutes, resulting in improved running mechanics and less stress on your QL. You’ll need a long, looped resistance band.

Sources indicate that sometimes, despite your best at-home efforts to treat an irritated QL, it’s still best to get checked out by a physical therapist. Haas recommends booking a PT appointment if you try the above stretches and strength moves and don’t see improvements after about two weeks.

Sources indicate that agnew suggests getting evaluated by a PT if you’re in so much pain that it’s inhibiting your running. In this case, getting seen sooner can help mitigate pain before further challenges arise, Agnew explains.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nike announced a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a upcoming method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear.
  • The significant highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nike announced a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a upcoming method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear. But the most interesting product unveiling is the Vaporfly 5—Nike is calling it the “most aggressive Vaporfly yet.”.

The significant highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it. “At the center of Vaporfly 5 is a fresh, wave-shaped Flyplate,” Nike’s announcement read. “A ripple through the midfoot creates a spring-like sensation under the arch.”.

I got a look at the prototype in Chicago last month, when I visited Nike’s headquarters during marathon weekend. There, I asked Bret Schoolmeester, vice president of running footwear product, if he was concerned about calling the shoe a spring. He is not, and told me that shoes basically serve as springs already given the bouncy modern foams being used.

Sources indicate that remember back to the first carbon-plated shoes, when much of the uproar around them was because people believed the plates would act like springs. That’s not really what came to fruition, as we found that the plates basically were used as stiffening mechanisms to create leverage.

World Athletics rules permit a plate in a single layer, and that’s what Nike is technically creating here. The difference is in the shaping. The bump in this upcoming plate, combined with the midsole geometry, will allow the plate to flex when you land and snap back to shape to propel you ahead.

Industry observers note that nike also looked at ways to strip weight, which you can see through the massive carve-outs in the foam, the super thin Vapor Mesh upper, and sparse use of Goatek outsole. Another weight-saving measure is adding ZoomX LT, the lightweight version of ZoomX that we saw in the Alphafly 4. A thin layer of that sits between the plate and your foot, while the standard ZoomX is used between the plate and the road for control and responsiveness.

It has been revealed that with these changes, Nike is positioning this shoe to be a shorter-distance road racing shoe. Given the overhaul of the Alphafly 4 and the announcement of the Apex, a hyper shoe designed for elite marathoners, the Vaporfly is being pitched for races up to 13.1 miles. Sure, some runners will lace it up for a full marathon, though it’s going to be lighter and snappier to excel at faster speeds.

The shoe won’t be available until “fall 2027,” but Nike is showing it off early as it drums up excitement for upcoming footwear and apparel at its World of Athletes event.

Beyond the Vaporfly 5, there were some other cool latest innovations announced, including “Tuned Air.” Through a new manufacturing process, Nike is able to create lighter Air units more rapidly, which can be customized for various applications.

I spoke with Phil McCartney, executive vice president, chief innovation, design and product officer, last week about Tuned Air. He explained that through a proprietary digital print and selective lamination process, Air units can be created with different amounts of cushioning and support. Those characteristics are delivered not only through the physical geometries of the Air unit, but also by varying the pressure within each unit.

Industry observers note that nike has previously talked about “Tuned Air,” and we saw it in use with the Pegasus Plus 2. But that was really just offering a few different air bags. The idea is that bigger shoes are worn by bigger runners and, thus, bigger Air units with greater gas pressures are required. So, shoes any smaller than a women’s 7.5 (M6) got an Air unit that’s 9.5 mm thick with 15 psi. Moving on up to a men’s 10.5 (W12), the bag gains 2 mm thickness. And, those runners with larger feet sit atop the 11.5mm-thick unit pumped up with 20 psi.

In a recent development, these new units, however, are different altogether. Nike found a way to remove the need for pins and rigid zones that formed the Air units, so that each can offer better cushioning and responsiveness.

Like the Vaporfly 5, Tuned Air won’t make an appearance until later in 2027. The prototype shoe teased in the image above has one massive Air unit making up the entire midsole. No word yet on which model or franchise that shoe will reside.

While we wait, the fastest Nike available to any of us remains the Alphafly 4.

Jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

💡 Key Takeaways
